This prohibition is applicable to listed companies. The Department of Company Affairs vide its Circular No. 9/94 (Circular Letter No. 17/32/93 - CL V dated September 6,1994) has also prohibited issue of bonus shares out of revaluation reserve by the existing private/ closely-held and unlisted companies.

The Guidance note on availability of revaluation reserve for issue of bonus shares issued by the ICAI (Published in November 1994 issue of the Chartered Accountant) argues that the excess of the revalued amount over the net book value of fixed assets, which is credited to revaluation reserve, is created as a result of book adjustment only. The revaluation reserve does not result from an arm's length transaction; it represents an expert's perception of value. The revaluation reserve thus does not represent realised gain.

The ICAI Guidance Note also states that share capital represents money or money's worth received from the owners and capitalisation of earned profits or other gains arising out of arm's length transactions. It is a cardinal principle that only such profits as are earned or the relevant capital receipts (e.g. share premium) as are realised, can be capitalised.

6.2 Expert's value perception - So long as the expert's perception of the fair value of a fixed asset is judicious, there is nothing wrong in depending on such valuation, in case the upper limit of revaluation is restricted to the net recoverable amount. Substitution of historical cost becomes necessary when it materially differs from the fair value of the fixed assets. A going concern may not think of disposing of a particular asset, still the increase in value of the asset, although unrealised, cannot be denied. Since the revaluation reserve forms part of the shareholders' funds, it should be treated as a free reserve.

6.3 Arm's length transactions and business income -The concept of arm's length relationship is altogether irrelevant in this context. The reported net profit of an entity is not necessarily the result of arm's length transactions. Also it is not necessary for the purpose of a bonus issue to consider to what extent the accumulated surplus of the entity has resulted from arm's length transactions.

6.4 Unrealised gain - Of course, the revaluation reserve represents unrealised gain. But it represents real gain and cannot be treated as a fictitious gain. Accordingly, the shareholders should not be denied the right to utilise any such real gain in the manner they want. It is not unknown to the shareholders that such a bonus issue, if any, results from unrealised gain.

6.5 Accounting effect of bonus issue - Presently, many companies take a transfer from the revaluation reserve to the extent of additional depreciation. To that extent profit is inflated every year and the revaluation reserve is converted into the so called 'earned profit'. It is just a matter of time to convert revaluation reserve into 'earned profit' and as soon as the conversion is complete there is no bar on utilising such 'earned profit' for issuing bonus shares.

In case the revaluation reserve is utilised for a bonus issue, the company would have no choice but to charge additional depreciation out of profit.

6.6 Corporate freedom - One of the basic tenets of economic liberalisation is reduction/elimination of bureaucratic interference on the activities of private entrepreneurs. Corporate management should be given freedom to adopt a suitable financial management policy. A bonus issue out of the revaluation reserve will not generally be supported by increase in the earning capacity. However, the management will not find difficulty in maintaining the dividend rate in real terms. A decline in post-equity pricewill have no effect in real terms, since this book adjustment has no effect on the earnings of the entity.

They do not replace the concept of 'income' or 'expenditure', as normally understood in the Act, for the purposes of Chapter X. The meaning had to be obtained from the plain language of a taxing statute. If there was ambiguity with regard to either the subject of the tax, the person liable to pay the tax or the rate of tax to be paid, then there was no tax chargeable under that law.

Introduction

Buy-back of Shares and Company Law

RAJESH DHAWAN

The author is MBA, Finance

In this write-up, the issue for consideration is buy-back of shares under Company Law. After citing relevant provisions, the author has highlighted the conditions for buy-back and prohibition for buy-back in certain circumstances.

INTRODUCTION

1. Not only statute, but also common law, has upheld the ‘sanctity’ of a company’s capital. In 1887, in Trevor v. Whitworth 12 App. Case 409, it was held that a company limited by shares may not purchase its own shares as this would amount to an unauthorized reduction of capital. The rationale for this decision is plain, namely, that the creditors of the company make decisions on its credit-worthiness on several grounds, but an important ground is the amount of its share capital. If the Courts had not established at an early stage that capital was ‘sacrosanct’ and could not be returned to shareholders at their whim, then share capital would not have been protected. Without this protection, creditors could find shareholders depleting share capital, with creditors left to carry all business risks.

RELEVANT PROVISIONS

2. In India, the rule in Trevor v. Whitworth was enshrined in section 77 of the Companies Act, 1956 which prohibited a company from buying or cancelling its own shares, unless it complied with the provisions and followed the procedure for reduction of share capital under sections 100 to 104 of the Companies Act, which involved confirmation by the Court.

However, section 77A of the Companies Act, which was inserted in the Companies Act by the Companies (Amendment) Act, 1999 with retrospective effect from October 31, 1998, is an exception to the prohibition under section 77 and section 100. Section 77A allows companies to buy-back their own shares as well as other specified securities.

Section 77(1) provides that a company limi-ted by shares or a company limited by guarantees having a share capital cannot buy its own shares, as it involves permanent reduction of capital without sanction of the Court.

However, the Companies (Amendment) Act, 1999, has introduced three new sections, viz., sections 77A, 77AA and 77B whereunder companies have been permitted to buy-back their shares or other securities subject to certain conditions. Besides, the SEBI has issued certain guidelines regulating these buy-backs. The provisions relating to buy-back as per the Amendment Act including SEBI guidelines in this regard are as follows :—

Section 77A, inserted by the (Amendment) Act, 1999, allows [subject to provision of section 77B(2)] a company to buy its own shares out of :—

(i) its free reserves; or

(ii) the security premium account; or

(iii) the proceeds of any share or other specified securities.

However, no buy-back of any kind of shares or other specified securities shall be made out of the proceeds of an earlier issue of the same kind of shares or same kind of other specified securities.

In case shares are bought back out of free reserves, then a sum equal to the nominal value of shares bought back shall be transferred to a reserve account to be called the capital redemption reserve account (section 77AA). The details of such transfer shall be disclosed in the balance sheet. The SEBI guidelines stipulate that this account shall be disclosed in the balance sheet. The SEBI guidelines stipulate that this account shall be allowed to be used for issue of fully paid bonus shares.

CONDITIONS FOR BUY-BACK

3. Following are the conditions for buy-back :—

A. Section 77A(2) provides that no company shall purchase its own shares or other specified securities unless :—

(a) the buy-back is authorised by its articles;

(b) a special resolution has been passed in general meeting of the company authorising the buy-back;

The Companies (Amendment) Act, 2001 (with effect from October 23, 2001) has authorised the buy-back by passing a resolution at a meeting of the board of directors, provided the buy-back does not exceed 10 per cent of the total paid-up equity capital and free reserves of the company. However, there cannot be more than one such buy-back in any period of 365 days.

(c) the buy-back is less than 25 per cent of the total paid-up capital and free reserves of the company purchasing its own shares or other specified securities. However, the buy-back of equity shares in any financial year must not exceed 25 per cent of its paid up equity capital in that financial year;

3. Preference shareholder cannot maintain an insolvency petition u/s 7 as CRPS funds are share capital not debt: SC

EPC Constructions India Ltd. v. Matix Fertilizers and Chemicals Ltd. [2025] 179 taxmann.com 650 (SC) In the instant case, the appellant, acting as an engineering, procurement and construction contractor, had entered into contracts with the respondent for setting up a fertiliser complex, under which an amount of about ?572.7 crores became due. The parties thereafter discussed conversion of a part of the outstanding receivables into a subordinate debt. Pursuant to this, the respondent proposed conversion of up to ?400 crores of the outstanding dues into preference shares.

The appellant's board approved conversion into 8% Cumulative Redeemable Preference Shares (CRPS), and the respondent allotted 25 crore CRPS of ?10 each aggregating to ?250 crores, carrying a cumulative dividend of 8% and redeemable at par at the end of three years, with an option to redeem earlier at the issuer's discretion. The appellant accepted the allotment and the CRPS were issued accordingly.

On expiry of the redemption period, the appellant filed an application under section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code claiming about ?310 crores as payable on maturity of the CRPS. The NCLT dismissed the application, and the NCLAT, by the impugned order, dismissed the appeal.

The Supreme Court held that the fact that the redemption period of the CRPS had expired did not lend greater weight to the appellant's case. It held that the appellant, being a preference shareholder, was not a creditor and, therefore, an application under section 7 was not maintainable. The Court further held that accounting treatment of the transaction, based on accounting standards, would not be determinative of the nature of the relationship between the parties, which had to be gathered from the documents executed between them.

The Court held that the paid-up money on shares constitutes share capital and does not amount to debt. It further held that shares could be redeemed only out of profits or out of amounts set aside for payment of dividends, which was not the situation in the present case, and therefore the argument that redemption was due was not meritorious. Accordingly, the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal.

5. ARGUMENTS BEFORE THE HIGH COURT 6. HIGH COURT'S VERDICT

The Bombay High Court held that on the facts of the present case, issue of shares at a premium by VISL to its non-resident AE does not give rise to any income from an admitted international transaction and thus, Indian Transfer Pricing provisions are not applicable for the following reasons:

Income arising from an international transaction is a pre-condition for application of Transfer Pricing provisions. Further, the Act defines the term income in an inclusive manner. Income, in its normal meaning, will not include capital receipts unless specifically provided. The amounts received on issue of share capital including the premium are on capital account. In this case, what is being sought to be taxed is capital forgone i.e. not received from a non-resident in the form of short premium. Therefore, absent express legislation, an amount received, accrued or arising on capital account transactions cannot be subjected to tax as income.

The High Court further held that the transaction on capital account or on account of restructuring would become taxable to the extent it impacts income i.e., under-reporting of interest received/over reporting of interest paid or claiming of depreciation. It is that income (and not the capital receipt) which is to be determined having regard to the ALP under the Transfer Pricing provisions.

The Transfer Pricing provisions are brought into statute books to ensure that the transaction is taxed only on the income computed as per the ALP of the transaction and to ensure that there is no manipulation of prices/consideration between AEs.

In any case, the entire exercise of taxing the amounts allegedly not received as share premium fails, as no tax is charged on the amount received as share premium.

Neither the capital receipts received by VISL on issue of equity shares to its AE nor the shortfall between the alleged FMV of its equity shares and the issue price of the equity shares can be considered as income within the meaning of the expression as defined in the Act and hence not subject to Transfer Pricing provisions in India.

The reasoning that if the ALP were received, the Taxpayer would be able to invest the same and earn income, proceeds on a mere surmise/assumption and that this cannot be the basis of taxation.

The Tax Authorities relied on this section to argue that differences between the ALP and the price charged for issue of shares is the benefit conferred upon the holding company.

Relying on section 92(2) of the Act is misplaced. Section 92(2) of the Act, which deals with a situation where two or more AEs enter into an arrangement whereby they are to receive any benefit, service or facility then the allocation, apportionment or contribution of the corresponding cost or expenditure is to be determined for each AE based on ALP, is meant to cover cases of cost sharing arrangements and/or cost contribution arrangements. Section 92(2) would have no application in cases like the present one, where there is no occasion to allocate, apportion or contribute any cost and/or expenses between the Taxpayer and its AE. Ignoring words in a statute to achieve a predetermined objective is not permissible and the same would amount to re-drafting the legislation, which is beyond the jurisdiction of the Courts.

The contention of the Tax Authorities that in view of the Transfer Pricing provisions, notional income is to be taxed and real income is not relevant is unacceptable. The entire exercise of determining the ALP is only to arrive at the real income earned.

Even income arising from international transactions between AEs must satisfy the test of income per se under the Act and must find its home under one of the charging provisions. It is a re-computation exercise to be carried out only when income arises in case of an international transaction between AEs. It does not warrant recomputation of a consideration received/given on capital account except in cases of interest paid/received on loans taken/given, depreciation taken on machinery, etc. Therefore, in the absence of a charging provision to tax issue of shares at a premium to a non-resident, the occasion to invoke the computational Transfer Pricing provisions does not arise.

Further, in view of inclusion of issue of shares, by a company to another resident, at a price in excess of FMV in the definition of income under the Act, there is conscious intention of the Parliament to not tax amounts received from a non-resident for issue of shares, as it would discourage capital inflow from abroad.

The High Court has been rightly able to distinguish between the 'income' per se and the capital which is primarily the source to earn income. One important take away from the decision is the High Court's acknowledgement that mere reporting of an international transaction out of abundant caution would not make the same taxable if there is no income arising from such international transaction.

('Vodafone') to its holding company at value less than those determined by the AO and TPO, which resulted in shortfall of premium of around 1,308 crores. The issue that arose before the Bombay High Court was whether the alleged shortfall in share premium arising out of the issuance of shares by 'Vodafone' to its holding company constituted 'income' chargeable to tax in the hands of 'Vodafone'? The High Court again held in favour of 'Vodafone' as under:

(a)

Whether capital account transaction could be charged to tax: The amount received on issue of shares is admittedly a capital account transaction not separately brought within the definition of Income, except in cases covered by Section 56(2)(viib) of the Act. Thus, such capital account transaction not falling within a statutory exception could not be brought to tax.In tax jurisprudence, it is well-settled that following four factors are essential ingredients to a taxing statute:

(a)

Subject of tax;

(b)

Person liable to pay the tax;

(c)

Rate at which tax is to be paid, and

(d)

Measure or value on which the rate is to be applied.

There is difference between a charge to tax and the measure of tax as mentioned in (a) and (d) above. This distinction was brought out by the Supreme Court in Bombay Tyres India Ltd. v. Union of India [1984] 1 SCC 467 wherein it was held that the charge of excise duty is on manufacture while the measure of the tax is the selling price of the manufactured goods.

In this case, the charge was on income as understood in the Act, and where income arises from an International Transaction, than the measure is to be found on application of ALP so far Chapter X of the Act is concerned.

Thus, arriving at the transactional value/consideration on the basis of ALP does not convert non-income into income. The tax can be charged only on income and in the absence of any income arising, the issue of applying the measure of ALP to transactional value/consideration itself does not arise.

The ingredient (a) above is not satisfied, i.e., subject of tax is income which is chargeable to tax. The issue of shares at a premium is a capital account transaction and not income.

(b)

Whether Chapter X of the Income-tax Act includes a charging provision to tax issue of shares at a premium as income: On contention of the revenue that Chapter X of the Act is a complete Code by itself and not merely a machinery provision to compute the ALP and, therefore, hidden benefit arising out of the transaction of issue shares to AE should be charged to tax as the charging section is inherent in Chapter X of the Act, the High Court held as under:

i.

It is well-settled position, in law, that a charge to tax must be mentioned specifically in the Act. In the absence of there being a charging Section in Chapter X of the Act, it is not possible to read a charging provision into Chapter X of the Act. There is no charge express or implied in letter or in spirit to tax issue of shares at a premium as income.

ii.

Chapter X of the Act is a machinery provision to arrive at the ALP of a transaction between AEs. The substantive charging provisions are found in Sections 4, 5, 15 (Salaries), 22 (Income from house property), 28 (Profits and gains of business), 45 (Capital gain) and 56 (Income from other Sources).

iii.

Even Income arising from International Transaction between AE must satisfy the test of Income under the Act and must find its home in one of the above heads, i.e., charging provisions which revenue had not been able to show.

iv.

In the present case, there was no charging provision to tax capital account transaction in respect of issue of shares at a premium and computation provisions could not replace/ substitute the charging provisions.

v.

Thus, issue of shares at a premium by Vodafone to its non-resident holding company did not give rise to any income from an admitted International Transaction. So, no occasion to apply Chapter X of the Act can arise in such a case.

Some areas of doubt

13. In the interpretation of section 115AD of the Act, doubts are bound to arise in quite a few areas. Two such areas of doubt are dealt with below:

(i) In the case of renunciation of rights offer for a consideration, a doubt may arise whether the resulting gain will fall within the purview of section 115AD of the Act. The extreme view that could possibly be taken is that such gain cannot be treated as "income received in respect of securities", nor as "income by way of short-term capital gain", with the result that the rates prescribed in section 115AD of the Act cannot be applied. While there cannot be any doubt that such gain cannot be treated as "income by way of capital gain" as contemplated in section 115AD of the Act, there is no reason why it cannot be treated as "income received in respect of securities" as envisaged in that provision. In Union of India v. Vijay Chand Jain [1977] 47 Comp. Cas. 674, the Supreme Court observed that the expression "in respect of" in its widest sense, means "connected with". Undoubtedly, the rights offer is connected with the holding of the specified securities, and hence any gain arising by its exploitation can be construed as "income received in respect of securities".

(ii ) Another area of doubt that may arise is about the applicability of section 115AD of the Act to a FII who is a dealer in shares and securities, and not an investor. The question that would arise in such a case is whether the profits arising to a FII from the business of dealing in shares and securities can be treated as "income in respect of securities" as envisaged in section 115AD of the Act. One line of thinking is that such profits not per se arise from the securities, but they arise from the business of dealing in securities, and hence the concessional rate of 20 per cent cannot be applied. With due respect, the author bags to differ from this view. The clue to the problem can be found in the wordings of section 115AD themselves. It states, inter alia, that in the computation of income received in respect of the securities, no deductions under sections 28 to 44C will be allowed. These provisions in the Act deal with the deductions available in the computation of business income. 2. IS SHARE INFUSION AN 'INTERNATIONAL TRANSACTION'?

Section 922 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (the Act) requires that any income, allowance for any expenses (including allocations) and allowance for any interest, arising out of international transactions should be computed having regard to the arm's length price.

The question is whether share infusion falls within the definition of the term 'international transaction' under section 92B of the Act. It may be mentioned that the term 'international transaction' as originally defined covered a wide gamut of transactions (including transactions having a bearing on assets) entered into between two associated enterprises (out of which, at least one should be a non-resident). By the Finance Act, 2010, an explanation was added to further extend the scope of this term. This extended definition was made retrospectively effective from the day the Indian Transfer Pricing Regulations were introduced i.e. April 1, 2001.

This extended definition includes a clause, which reads as follows:

'(e) a transaction of business restructuring or reorganisation, entered into by an enterprise with an associated enterprise, irrespective of the fact that it has bearing on the profit, income, losses or assets of such enterprises at the time of the transaction or at any future date'

The term 'business restructuring' or 'reorganisation' have not been defined in the Act and hence prone to a wider interpretation. It is possible that the tax department may seek to infer that these terms cover any change in shareholding, including share infusion. Even without resorting to the extension of the definition, a view is possible that 'share' is a form of an 'assets' and hence, any change in the value of shares, would impact the assets of a taxpayer. Therefore, it can be said that share infusion stands covered by the original definition of the term international transaction.

28.19 Regulation 96 of Table A provides for capitalization of profits to say that the company in general meeting may, upon the recommendation of the Board, resolve to capitalize any part of the amount for the time being standing to the credit of any of the company’s reserve accounts, or to the credit of the profit and loss account, or otherwise available for distribution, in kind, amongst the members who would have been entitled to it if distributed by way of dividend and in same proportions, sections 78(2) and 80(5). Such amount is available to be applied either in or towards paying up any amount for the time being unpaid on any shares held by each such member, or paying up in full un-issued shares of the company to be allotted and distributed, credited as fully paid-up, to and amongst such members in their respective proportions, or partly in one way and partly the other. However, a share premium account or a capital redemption reserve account can be applied only in the paying up of un-issued shares to be issued to members of the company as fully paid bonus shares to the members according to their respective entitlements but not as a gift, CIT v. Chunilal Khusaldas [1974] 44 Comp. Cas. 90 (Guj.). This accords with the Proviso to section 205(3), saying that the requirement of the Act for payment of dividend in cash in no way prohibits the capitalization of profits or reserves of a company for the purpose of issuing fully paid-up bonus shares or paying up any amount for the time being unpaid on any shares held by the members of the company. The effect of issue of bonus shares from general reserves is to seal off the chances of the amounts being available for distribution as dividend permanently by conversion into share capital without contribution from the shareholders. According to the decision of Supreme Court in Shree Gopal Paper Mills Ltd. v. CIT AIR 1970 SC 1750, bonus shares become vested from the date of the resolution in general meeting and not from the date of subsequent allotment by the Board of directors. For issue of bonus shares, see discussion in Ch 20.

In general, if there is a provision in the articles corresponding to Regulations 96 and 97 of Table A - which only deal with capitalization of profits—any company limited by shares may capitalise profits available for distribution as dividend by issue of fully paid bonus shares and issue the same to the existing members pro rata. From the DCA Circular 9/1994 dated 6-9-1994 it would appear that the guidelines for issue of bonus shares issued by SEBI under the SEBI (DIP) Guidelines, 2000 for listed companies are applicable to all companies—that is to say, that bonus shares are to be issued out of free general reserves built out of genuine profits or share (securities?) premium account collected in cash, but not out of reserves created by revaluation of fixed assets. Issue of bonus shares has the effect of reducing the share value proportionately in the ratio of its issue, Chandrakant Mulraj v. Tata Engg. & Locomotive Co. Ltd. [1985] 58 Comp. Cas. 320 (Bom.); and the character of bonus shares in the hands of the shareholders is capital but not dividend : IRC v. Blott (1921) 2 AC 171 (HL).

Securities premium account and capital redemption account for bonus shares - A securities premium account and a capital redemption reserve account may be used for purpose of issue of fully paid bonus shares - Regulation 39(ii)(D) of Model Articles of Association Table-F of Companies Act, 2013.

7.3-3 Board to act on the basis of ordinary resolution in general meeting Bonus shares are first approved in the meeting of Board. Once bonus issued is announced on basis of Board resolution, the company cannot subsequently withdraw the same - Rule 14 of Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014.

The company in general meeting, upon recommendation of Board, can pass following resolution as ordinary resolution - (a) that it is desirable to capitalise any part of the amount for the time being standing to the credit of any of the company's reserve accounts, or to the credit of the profit and loss account, or otherwise available for distribution; and (b) that such sum (capitalized profit) be accordingly set free for distribution in the manner specified in Regulation 39(ii) amongst the members who would have been entitled thereto, if distributed by way of dividend and in the same proportions [Regulation 39(i) of Model Articles of company limited by shares as contained in Table-F of Schedule I of Companies Act, 2013].

After such ordinary resolution, Board can give effect to the resolution by doing all necessary acts [Articles 39(ii)(E) and 40 of Model Articles of company limited by shares as contained in Table-F of Schedule I of Companies Act, 2013].

7.3-4 Fractional certificate or payment of cash

The ratio of issue of bonus shares may be such that some members may be entitled to fractional share.

In such case, the Board may make provisions in respect of such fractional entitlement (a) by the issue of fractional certificates or (b) by payment in cash or (c) otherwise as it thinks fit [Regulation 40(ii)(a) of Model Articles of company limited by shares as contained in Table-F of Schedule I of Companies Act, 2013].

For this purpose, Board may authorise any person to enter into an agreement with the company for the allotment to the members additional shares credited as fully paid up. Alternatively, company can pay, on behalf of members to any unpaid amount on their existing shares [Regulation 40(ii)(b) of Model Articles of company limited by shares as contained in Table-F of Schedule I of Companies Act, 2013].

Such agreement is binding on the members.

Normally, such fractional rights are consolidated into shares and sold by the person authorised by the Board. The proceeds are then distributed among members in proportion to their fractional rights.

7.3-5 Effect of issue of bonus shares

Bonus shares is an excellent way of bringing the paid up capital of the company in line with actual capital employed in the business. It broadens the capital base and improves image of the company.

Only fully paid bonus shares can be issued. Partly paid bonus shares cannot be issued, as it will create liability on members which they may not want.

Bonus shares are same as normal shares and members are entitled to get dividend on such shares. They can also sell the shares, if they wish. A bonus share is thought of as a gift from the company. In fact, a bonus issue simply divides the existing shares into smaller units e.g. assume that equity share capital of company is Rs. one crore and free reserves are Rs. 2.5 crores. The company is declaring dividend of 30%. If bonus shares in ratio of 1:1 are issued, the share capital will be Rs. 2 crores and free reserves will be reduced to 1.5 crores. Thus, actually, there is neither any cash payment to members nor any cash receipt from members. If market price of shares was Rs. 100 per share before issue of bonus shares, it will come down to Rs. 50 per share. Thus, the shareholder is neither a loser nor a gainer. If the company now declares 15% dividend, the shareholder will get the same amount which he was getting earlier.

Issuance of bonus shares is nothing but mere capitalisation of the profits of company in respect of which certificates are issued to the shareholders entitling them to participate in the amount of reserve but only as part of capital - Hunsur Plywood Works v. CIT (1997) 95 Taxman 460 = 229 ITR 112 (SC) - quoted with approval in Khoday Distilleries Ltd. v. CIT (2009) 176 Taxman 142 (SC), where it was held that there is no element of gift in a company issuing bonus shares.

like to have more working capital but it need not go into the market for obtaining fresh capital by issuing fresh shares. The necessary money is available with it and this money is converted into shares which really means that the undistributed profits have been ploughed back into the business and converted into share capital. Therefore, fully paid bonus shares are merely a distribution of capitalized undivided profit. It would be a misnomer to call the recipients of bonus shares as donees of shares from the company.' As the above decision was in the context of section 4(1)(a) of the Gift-tax Act, 1958 which was also based on taxing transactions involving 'inade-quate consideration' like section 56(2)(x)(c)(B) of the Act, a view can be taken that bonus shares cannot also be taxed under section 56(2)(x)(c)(B). Besides the Explanatory Memorandum to the Finance Bill, 2010 clarifies that 'The provisions of section 56(2)(vii) were introduced as a counter evasion mechanism to prevent laundering of unaccounted income under the garb of gifts, particularly after abolition of the Gift-tax Act. The provisions were intended to extend the tax net to such transactions in kind.' Issue of bonus shares and its receipt by shareholders is legitimate corporate action under the Companies Act, 1956 [now the Companies Act, 2013] and certainly cannot be called 'laundering of unaccounted income under the garb of gifts'. Thus, the above clarification seems to fortify the view that bonus shares cannot also be taxed under section 56(2)(x)(c)(B).

When there is an issue of bonus shares, money remains with company and nothing comes to shareholders as there is no transfer of property, and thus, provisions of section 56(2)(vii)(c) are not attracted. The issue which arises for consideration in this appeal is 'as to whether the fair market value of bonus shares computed as per Rule 11U and Rule 11UA of the Income-tax Rules can be considered as income from other sources as per section 56(2)(vii) of the Act. A careful scrutiny of section 56(2)(vii) of the Act contemplates two contingencies firstly, where the property is received without consideration and secondly, where it is received for consideration less than the fair market value. The issue of bonus shares by capitalization of reserves is merely a reallocation of the companies funds. There is no inflow of fresh funds or increase in the capital employed, which remains the same. The total funds available with the company remains the same and issue of bonus shares does not result in any change in respect of capital structure of the company. Thus, there is no addition or alteration to the profit making apparatus and the total funds available with the company remain the same. In substance, when a shareholder gets a bonus shares, the value of the original share held by him goes down and the market value as well as intrinsic value of two shares put together will be the same or nearly the same as per the value of original share before the issue of bonus shares. Thus, any profit derived by the assessee on account of receipt of bonus shares is adjusted by depreciation in the value of equity shares held by him. In the instant case, there is no material on record to infer that bonus shares have been transferred with an intention to evade tax, which is the object of the provision in question. Therefore, the CIT (Appeals) as well as the tribunal have rightly held that when there is an issue of bonus shares, the money remains with the company and nothing comes to the shareholders as there is no transfer of the property and the provisions of section under section 56(2)(vii)(c) of the Act are not attracted to the fact situation of the case. 8.4

DIMINUTION OF CAPITAL DOES NOT CONSTITUTE REDUCTION OF CAPITAL

As per section 61(1)(e) of Companies Act, 2013 [Corresponding to section 94(1)(e) of the 1956 Act], a company can cancel shares which have not been taken or agreed to be taken by any person, and diminish the amount of its share capital by the amount so cancelled.

Section 61(2) of Companies Act, 2013 [Corresponding to section 94(3) of the 1956 Act] states that such cancellation is not 'reduction of capital'.

The section is applicable only to change in memorandum. The Memorandum specifies only 'Authorised Capital'. Hence, only 'Authorised Capital' can be cancelled under this section.

Such reduction in authorised capital in Memorandum is not likely to be of much use, as stamp duty paid on authorised capital will not be refunded. Hence, this provision is hardly used.

8.4-1 Issues relating to income tax if amount distributed to members on reduction of capital

As per section 2(22)(d) of Income Tax Act, any distribution to its shareholders by a company on the reduction of its capital, to the extent to which the company possesses accumulated profits (whether capitalised or not) shall be treated as dividend at the hands of shareholders. If any part of capital is returned, it is not 'deemed dividend' [see CIT v. Urmila Ramesh (1998) 230 ITR 422 = 96 Taxman 533 (SC)].

Dividend Distribution Tax will be payable on such dividend.

In CIT v. G. Narasimhan (1999) 102 Taxman 66 (SC), it was held that amount distributed by a company on reduction of its share capital has two components - distribution attributable to accumulated profits and distribution attributed to capital (except capitalised profits). To the extent of accumulated profits in the hands of company (whether capitalised or not), the return to the shareholder on reduction of its share capital is a return of such accumulated profits. This part would be taxable as dividend. The balance may be subject to tax as capital gains that accrue.

In Kartikeya v. Sarabhai [1997] 94 Taxman 94 = 228 ITR 163 = (1997) 7 SCC 524 = AIR 1997 SC 3794 = 1997 AIR SCW 3646, it was held that in case of reduction of share capital, amount paid to shareholder results in extinguishment of his right. It is exigible to capital gains tax.

Bonus shares

Profits and other available reserves are capitalized and applied in paying up unissued shares or debentures, which are issued to the existing shareholders in proportion to their entitlement to dividends. The effect is that, in contrast to a dividend which reduces the assets of a company, a bonus issue does not reduce those assets since the assets and liabilities side of the balance sheet remains unchanged but the capital and the reserve side of the balance sheet is rearranged with a reduction in the amount of profits and other relevant reserves and an equal increase in the amount of the paid up share capital reflecting the increase in the issued share capital (see Hill v. Permanent Trustee Co. of New South Wales Ltd. 1930 AC 720, per Lord Russell)

When a shareholder gets a bonus share the value of the original share held by him goes down. In effect, the shareholder gets two shares instead of the one share held by him and the market value as well as the intrinsic value of the two shares put together will be the same or nearly the same as the value of the original share before the bonus issue.” Thus, in substance bonus shares represent capitalization of the profits and the right to receive profits embedded in the shares fructifies into the bonus shares. In other words, the shareholder receives something, which always belonged to him. To put it differently, it cannot be said that the shares are received from the company. In other words, realization of pre-existing rights cannot be regarded as receipts. In any case, as discussed earlier, creation and issue of shares do not constitute transfer by the company and accordingly the receipts by the shareholder.

Rights shares

1.13-13 Rights shares, so popularly referred, represent entitlement to the further issue of capital by a company, by way of inherent right. Section 81 of the Companies Act, 1956 so provides for any issue of shares (by a company), after expiry of two years from formation of a company or at any time after expiry of one year from the first allotment of shares, and lays down that:

“such further shares shall be offered to the persons who, at the time of the offer, are holders of the equity shares of the company, in proportion, as nearly as circumstances admit, to the capital paid-up on those shares at that date.” (Emphasis supplied).

Thus, in substance, rights shares represent right to receive further shares, which fructifies into issue and allotment thereof. In other words, the shareholder is allotted further shares, in terms of his pre-existing rights. Realization of pre-existing rights cannot be regarded as receipts. Further, allotment of rights shares, as such, does not affect the proportional interest, as also it does not have impact on the overall value of the holding of a shareholder. In any case, as discussed earlier, creation and issue of shares do not constitute a transfer by the company and accordingly the receipts by the shareholder.

Cost of acquisition

1.14 Section 49(4) of the Act provides for determining cost of acquisition of property (received without consideration or lower consideration) value whereof is taxed under the Clause. The value taken into account for the purposes of the Clause shall be deemed to be its cost.

To illustrate:

(a) A Ltd. has received the Shares without consideration. FMV thereof is, say, Rs. 100,000. It has paid tax thereon under the Clause. It sells the said shares for Rs. 125,000. For the purposes of computing capital gains, the cost of acquisition, in terms of the said provision, would be Rs. 100,000. Accordingly, the capital gains would be Rs. 25,000 (subject to applicability of indexed cost of acquisition).

(b) A Ltd. has purchased the Shares for Rs. 500,000. FMV thereof is Rs. 600,000. On the difference, it has paid tax under the Clause. It sells the same for Rs. 750,000. For computing capital gains, the cost of acquisition, in terms of the said provision, would be Rs. 600,000 being the value considered for the purposes of the Clause.

As said above, the value taxed under the Clause is adopted as cost and hence wherever applicable such cost can be indexed in terms of the provisions of the Act. It appears that the period of holding will have to be determined with reference to the date of receipt and, in particular, having regard to section 49(4).

For the purposes of computation of business income, the law is silent and there is no specific provision, like, section 49(4) providing for substitution of the value of property adopted for taxation under the Clause.

The Finance Act, 2010 has amended the above provisions as follows:

◆ Section 56(2)(vii)(b) is substituted with effect from 1-10-2009 effectively to delete sub-clause (b)(ii) to exclude the receipt of immovable property for an inadequate or lower consideration, which exceeds Rs. 50,000; and

- Bullion is included in the list of assets, with effect from 1-6-2010.

38.2

Whether allotment of bonus shares by a company to its shareholders will attract tax in shareholder's hands under section 56(2)(x)(c)?

If bonus shares can be regarded as received for free, i.e., without any consideration, then they would clearly attract tax under section 56(2)(x)(c)(A) if the aggregate fair market value of bonus shares received during the previous year along with all other items of shares and securities, jewellery etc. received without consideration during the previous year exceeds Rs. 50,000. The question arises whether it can be said that bonus shares can be said to have been received by the shareholder without consideration? In CIT v. Dalmia Investment Co. Ltd. [1964] 52 ITR 567 (SC), the Court held as under:

'Can we then say that the bonus shares are a gift and are acquired for nothing? At first sight, it looks as if they are so, but the impact of the issue of bonus shares has to be seen to realise that there is an immediate detriment to the shareholder in respect of his original holding…. by the issue of bonus shares pro rata, which ranked pari passu with the existing shares, the market price was exactly halved, and divided between the old and the bonus shares. This will ordinarily be the case but not when the shares do not rank pari passu and we shall deal with that case separately. When the shares rank pari passu the result may be stated by saying that what the shareholder held as a whole rupee coin is held by him, after the issue of bonus shares, in two 50 nP. coins. The total value remains the same, but the evidence of that value is not in one certificate but in two. …. The bonus shares can be valued by spreading the cost of the old shares over the old shares and the new issue taken together, if the shares rank pari passu. When they do not, the price may have to be adjusted either in the proportion of the face value they bear (if there is no other circumstances differentiating them) or on equitable considerations based on the market price before and after the issue.'

Interestingly, even section 55(2)(aa) of the Act (which provides that cost of acquisition of bonus shares shall be treated as 'Nil') does not refer to the bonus shares as 'shares received without consideration'. It only considers bonus shares as 'additional financial asset allotted to the assessee without any payment and on the basis of holding any other financial asset'. Thus, bonus shares are shares received 'without payment' and not 'without consideration'. Thus, it is possible to take a view that section 56(2)(x)(c)(A) is not attracted in case of receipt of bonus shares by a shareholder.

Therefore, a question would arise whether bonus shares received by any person can be taxed in his hands under section 56(2)(x)(c)(B)? In Khoday Distilleries Ltd. v. CIT [2009] 176 Taxman 142, the Supreme Court was seized of the question whether there was an element of 'gift' in the issue of bonus shares [in the context of section 4(1)(a) of the Gift-tax Act, 1958 which deemed property transferred for inadequate consideration as 'gift' under the said Act in the hands of the transferor/donor]. The said section 4(1)(a) provided that where property is transferred otherwise than for adequate consideration, the amount by which the value of the property as on the date of the transfer and determined in the manner laid down in Schedule II, exceeds the value of the consideration shall be deemed to be a gift made by the transferor. The Court held as under:

'13. When a company is prosperous and accumulates a large surplus, it converts this surplus into capital and divides the capital amongst the members in proportion to their rights. This is done by issuing fully paid shares representing the increased capital. The shareholders to whom the shares are allotted have to pay nothing. The purpose is to capitalize profits which may be available for division. Bonus shares go by the modern name of 'capitalization shares'. If the Articles of a company empowers the company, it can capitalize profits or reserves and issue fully paid shares of nominal value, equal to the amount capitalized, to its shareholders. The idea behind the issue of bonus shares is to bring the nominal share capital into line with the excess of assets over liabilities. A company would like to have more working capital but it need not go into the market for obtaining fresh capital by issuing fresh shares. The necessary money is available with it and this money is converted into shares which really means that the undistributed profits have been ploughed back into the business and converted into share capital. Therefore, fully paid bonus shares are merely a distribution of capitalized undivided profit. It would be a misnomer to call the recipients of bonus shares as donees of shares from the company.'

company on buyback of shares which are not listed on recognised stock exchange.

Prior to the amendments by Finance Act, 2016

(a)

distributed income was defined to mean the consideration paid by the company on buy back of shares as reduced by the amount which was received by the company for issue of such shares;

(b)

buyback had been defined to mean the purchase by a company of its own shares in accordance with the provisions of section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956. Thus the definition of buyback did not cover buybacks undertaken by a company under other provisions of the Companies Act, 1956 or the Companies Act, 2013.

Again there could be situations where shares may have been issued by the company in tranches, for different considerations, at different point of time or may have been issued in lieu of existing shares of another company under amalgamation, merger or demerger. In all these cases there was lack of clarity in determination of consideration received by the company at the time of issue of shares being bought back by the company (as per Explanatory Memorandum to Finance Bill, 2016).

In Capgemini India (P.) Ltd., In re [2016] 67 taxmann.com 1 (Bom.) it was held that the Indian company law, as it stood then, permitted a company to buy-back its shares either without Court approval (by adopting procedure of buy-back regulations) or with the Court's approval. If the law permitted a company to follow one of the two methods, it could not be compelled to follow only that method that results in higher tax liability. The Court held that the purchase of shares under section 391 of the Companies Act, 1956 (now section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013) was not covered by section 115QA.

In view of the above, section 115QA has been amended with effect from 1-6-2016 to provide that

(a)

Buyback will mean purchase by a company of its own shares in accordance with the provisions of any law for the time being in force relating to companies [Explanation (i) to section 115QA(1)].

(b)

Distributed income means the consideration paid by the company on buyback of shares as reduced by the amount, which was received by the company for issue of such shares, determined in the manner as may be prescribed [Explanation (ii) to section 115QA(1)].

7.5-1 'Purchase' of shares is a precondition

Even after the amendment in Explanation (i), 'purchase' of shares by a company is a precondition for applicability of section 115QA. If a particular transaction does not result in 'purchase' by the company, then section 115QA is not triggered.

Thus, section 115QA will now apply to buy backs under

(a)

sections 391 to 394 of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to sections 230 to 232 of the Companies Act, 2013);

(b)

section 395 of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to section 235 of the Companies Act, 2013);

(c)

section 402 of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to section 242(2)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013).

7.5-2 Unlisted share is a precondition

Even after the amendment, section 115QA applies only in respect of purchase of unlisted shares. The term 'shares' will include all types of shares including preference shares and convertible preference shares. However, listed shares or convertible debentures are not covered.

7.5-3 Positive distributed income

It appears that the provision envisages positive distributed income. If the consideration paid by the company on buyback of shares is less than the amount received by the company for issue of such shares than the distributed income would be negative and in these circumstances, obviously there will not be any liability under section 115QA.

7.5-4 Reduction of capital

Section 100 of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to section 66(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013) provides that a company may reduce the share capital and may 'pay off' any paid up share capital which is in excess of the wants of the company. According to one view, purchase of share under section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013) and reduction of capital under section 100 pursuant to which shares are 'transferred' to the company are two distinct transactions and such reduction cannot be construed as purchase of shares by the company within the meaning of section 115QA. In Goldman Sachs (India) Securities (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [ITA No. 3726 of 2015, decided on 12-2-2016] (Mum. - Trib.), the Tribunal cited observations from SEBI v. Sterlite Industries (India) Ltd. [2003] 45 SCL 475 (Bom.) and held that the observations of the Court did not leave any doubt that buyback of shares could not be equated with reduction of capital.

Buy back of shares

5.1 Section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956 permits a company to buy back its own shares upon fulfilment of the prescribed conditions. It has tax implications and broadly, there were two views :

◆ As per one view, utilisation of accumulated profits for the buy back, entailing reduction of capital, could amount to dividend attracting tax @ 10% under section 115-O of the Act in the hands of the company.

◆ As per the other view, the company is not liable to dividend tax inasmuch as the purchase of its own shares does not amount to reduction in capital and only the shareholders are liable to pay tax on the gains, if any.

To set the controversy at rest, the Finance Act, 1999 has made the following provisions :

(a) The payment made by a company for purchase of share would not constitute dividend [vide section 2(22)(iv)]; and

(b) Shareholders would be chargeable to capital gains tax (by inserting section 46A).

5.1-1 Dividend - Section 2(22) of the Act defines dividend inclusively. After listing the distribution or payment amounting to dividend, it lists certain distribution or payment not constituting dividend. In that list, the payment made by a company on purchase of its own shares from shareholder in terms of section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956 has been added [vide, sub-clause (iv)] meaning that such payment would not constitute dividend. Accordingly, the provisions of section 115-O of the Act would not apply.

However, this provision would not apply in respect of buy back of any shares or other securities by the company under any other provisions of the Companies Act, 1956 (i.e., other than section 77A) under any scheme of arrangement (e.g. an order under section 402 of the Companies Act, 1956) or otherwise. Accordingly, any payment made by the company in such a case for such purchase may constitute dividend within the meaning of section 2(22) of the Act.

5.1-2 Section 46A - The section provides as follows :

◆ When a shareholder or holder of other specified securities receives any consideration from a company,

◆ Upon purchase of its own shares or securities by the company,

◆ The difference between cost of acquisition and purchase price of shares or securities paid by the company would constitute capital gains,

◆ In computing the capital gains, section 48 should be given effect to,

◆ The gain would be chargeable to tax in the year of purchase and

◆ For the purpose, the other securities have the same meaning as assigned in Explanation to section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956.

5.1-2a Necessity - Shares or securities do constitute capital asset. It is settled law that upon purchase by the company, there is a transfer of shares [Anarkali Sarabhai v. CIT[1997] 224 ITR 422 (SC)]. Accordingly, any gain arising therefrom is chargeable to tax as capital gains or otherwise. Further, there was no controversy that a shareholder was liable to capital gains tax. Also, the question of reducing accumulated profit considered as dividend in computing the capital gain would not arise in view of the amendment made in section 2(22). In the circumstances, the need for a separate provision was not there. Also, the need for including other specified securities in the provision is also not clear.

7.5-3 Positive distributed income

It appears that the provision envisages positive distributed income. If the consideration paid by the company on buyback of shares is less than the amount received by the company for issue of such shares than the distributed income would be negative and in these circumstances, obviously there will not be any liability under section 115QA.

7.5-4 Reduction of capital Section 100 of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to section 66(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013) provides that a company may reduce the share capital and may 'pay off' any paid up share capital which is in excess of the wants of the company. According to one view, purchase of share under section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013) and reduction of capital under section 100 pursuant to which shares are 'transferred' to the company are two distinct transactions and such reduction cannot be construed as purchase of shares by the company within the meaning of section 115QA. In Goldman Sachs (India) Securities (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [ITA No. 3726 of 2015, decided on 12-2-2016] (Mum. - Trib.), the Tribunal cited observations from SEBI v. Sterlite Industries (India) Ltd. [2003] 45 SCL 475 (Bom.) and held that the observations of the Court did not leave any doubt that buyback of shares could not be equated with reduction of capital.

Further, the term used in section 66 is 'pay-off', which has been defined in Random House Dictionary as "to pay (someone) everything that is due to that person; To pay (debt) in full." Thus, the term 'pay-off' suggests that there is a due to the shareholder to the extent of his interest in the company that is been paid-off. It appears that this cannot be equated with purchase of shares in which there is nothing due to the seller till the sale transaction takes place.

According to the other view, the payment upon reduction is also purchase of shares. Section 2(22)(d) provides that dividend includes any distribution to its shareholders by a company on reduction of capital. However, the definition also provides that dividend does not include any payment made by a company on purchase of its own shares in accordance with the provisions of section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956. The fact that there is a specific exclusion of payment upon purchase of shares shows that in the absence of such exclusion, purchase of shares under section 77A could have been regarded as reduction of capital. Conversely, reduction of capital should also be construed as purchase of shares by the company.

It appears that the better view is that reduction of capital under section 66 of the Companies Act, 2013 is not a purchase within the meaning of section 115QA, although as a consequence of this view, the shareholder could be liable to

SUBSEQUENT ISSUE OF BONUS SHARES DOES AFFECT COST OF ACQUISITION

The Supreme Court in the case of Escorts Farms (Ramgarh) Ltd v. CIT [1996] 88 Taxman 453 (SC) held that when bonus shares are issued by a company, it has its impact on the original shares. The market value of the compa-ny's shares may get reduced to a figure nearer their nominal value. The value of the original shares acquired gets automatically reduced, notwithstanding the fact that the total holding of the shareholder may be larger. Where bonus shares are issued in re-spect of ordinary shares held in a company by an assessee who is a dealer in shares, their real cost to the assessee cannot be taken to be nil or their face value. They have to be valued by spreading the cost of the old shares over the old shares and the new issue (viz., the bonus shares) taken together if they rank pari passu and if they do not, the price may have to be adjusted either in proportion of the face value they bear (if there is no other circumstance to differen-tiate them) or on equitable considerations based on the market price before and after issue. There is no "dichotomy", as to whether the shares are held by an "investor" or "dealer" in shares. In both the cases, it is the surplus re-ceipt that is brought to tax, either as "capital gains" or "profit or loss", as the case may be, and in accordance with the relevant statutory provisions.

The following observations of the Supreme Court are rele-vant [From ITR Online]

"In Shekhawati General Traders Ltd. v. ITO [1971] 82 ITR 788 (SC), the court laid stress on the fact that the assessee had opted to take the cost of acquisition as provided by the relevant statute, i.e., the statutory cost of acquisition and thus substituting the market value as on January 1, 1954, in place of the actual cost of acquisition, and only in such a case, the subsequent issue of bonus shares cannot affect the issue. It is implicit from the above decision that the principle of averaging by spreading the cost over the old shares and the new bonus shares as enunciated by the Supreme Court in CIT v. Dalmia Investment Co. Ltd. [1964] 52 ITR 567 (SC) and other cases, will apply as a general rule in cases where the assessee claims to deduct the actual cost of acquisition, instead of the statutory cost of acquisition. It also stands to reason since the fair market value as per the "statutory cost of acquisition" will be a notional or fictional figure (mostly inflated) having no connection with the original or actual cost. It is after discussing the effect or impact of the issue of the bonus shares, on the value of the original shares generally and also the various possible methods for determining the cost of the bonus shares, that the Supreme Court in CIT v. Dalmia Investment Co. Ltd. case [1964] 52 ITR 567 (SC) stated that the real cost to the assessee of the bonus shares cannot be taken to be nil or their face value and they have to be valued by spreading the cost of the old shares over the old shares and the new issue (bonus shares), taken together, etc. The principle so laid down is one of general application."

7.3

BONUS SHARES

If a company is profit making, its accumulated profits and free reserves go on increasing. Thus, actual capital employed (i.e. share capital plus accumulated profit plus free reserves) is much higher than the share capital as reflected in the balance sheet. Hence, profits earned appear to be much higher compared to the share capital. Hence, part of accumulated profits and free reserves can be distributed among members as fully paid bonus shares.

A company may issue fully paid-up bonus shares to its members, out of — (i) its free reserves (ii) the securities premium account; or (iii) the capital redemption reserve account [section 63(1) of Companies Act, 2013] - similar provision in Regulation 39(ii)(D) of Model Articles of Association Table F of Companies Act, 2013.

Bonus shares out of securities premium account - Fully paid bonus shares can be issued out of securities premium account - section 52(2)(a) and 52(3)(a) of Companies Act, 2013 and Regulation 39(ii)(D) of the Table F of Companies Act, 2013.

Bonus shares out of capital redemption reserve account - If preference shares are redeemed out of profits, a sum equal to nominal amount of the shares to be redeemed are required to be transferred to capital redemption reserve account under section 55(2) of Companies Act, 2013. This capital redemption reserve account can be used to issue fully paid bonus shares to members - section 55(4) of Companies Act, 2013 and Regulation 39(ii)(D) of the Table F of Companies Act, 2013.

The capital redemption reserve arising out of buy back of securities can be utilised to issue fully paid bonus shares - section 69(2) of Companies Act, 2013.

No bonus out of revaluation of reserves - Bonus shares cannot be issued by capitalising reserves created by the revaluation of assets [proviso to section 63(1) of Companies Act, 2013] As per SEBI guidelines also, a listed company cannot use revaluation reserves to issue bonus shares.

SEBI guidelines for listed companies - SEBI guidelines for issue of bonus shares should be followed by a listed company.

Company can capitalise its profits or reserves for purpose of issue of bonus shares, if following conditions are fulfilled [section 63(2) of Companies Act, 2013] -

(a)

it is authorised by its articles.

(b)

it has, on the recommendation of the Board, been authorised in the general meeting of the company.

(c)

2.1 For the purpose of computing capital gains on sale/transfer of bonus shares, cost of acquisition of bonus shares has been hitherto taken on the basis of principles of spreading the cost of original shares over original and bonus shares as laid down by the Supreme Court in the case of CIT v. Dalmia Investment Co. Ltd [1964] 52 ITR 567.

The Finance Act, 1995, has amended section 55 with effect from assessment year 1996-97 to provide that the cost of bonus shares will be taken as nil for computation of capital gain on sale of bonus shares. This will not affect the cost of original shares. This procedure will also be applicable to any other security where a bonus issue has been made. Section 2(42A) has also been amended so as to provide that the period of holding of the bonus asset will be reckoned from the date of allotment of such asset. This amendment also comes into effect from 1-4-1996, i.e., assessment year 1996-97.

2.1-1 Determination of period of holding in case of bonus shares - On account of the fact that the cost of bonus shares is embedded in the cost of the original shares and also that the proportionate interest of a shareholder in a company remains the same after the issue of bonus shares, a legal controversy had arisen insofar as a view was expressed that the date of acquisition of bonus shares must relate back to the date of allotment of original shares. As per that view, although bonus shares were sold within a period of one year after its issue, the assessee, by relating the date of acquisition to the original shares, could claim long-term capital gains instead of short-term capital gains.

The Gujarat High Court in the case of CIT v. Chunilal Khushaldas [1974] 93 ITR 369 (Guj.) negatived such a claim and held that the date of issue of bonus shares must be considered as date of acquisition thereof. The Bombay High Court has also followed the said decision in the case of Manecklal Premchand v. CIT [1990] 186 ITR 554 (Bom.).

The aforesaid Court judgments are now given legislative recognition. Section 2(42A) has now been amended to provide that the date of acquisition of bonus shares (or any other bonus financial asset) will be the date of allotment of such bonus shares (or bonus financial asset).

Issue of bonus shares

Section 63 of the 2013 Act is a new enabling provision in the 2013 Act for issue of bonus shares subject to satisfaction of specified conditions. There was no such provision in the 1956 Act.

The proviso to sub-section (3) of section 205 of the 1956 Act permitted capitalization of profits or reserve of a company for the purpose of issuing fully paid up bonus shares or paying up any amount for the time being unpaid on any shares held by the members of the company. Thus, the 1956 Act specifically permitted utilization of reserve arising from revaluation of assets for purpose of issuing fully paid up bonus shares. In view of the aforesaid proviso, a company can issue bonus shares by capitalization of revaluation reserve if the Articles of Association of the company so permits. [Supreme Court's decision in Bhagwati Developers v. Peerless General Finance Investment Co. [2005] 62 SCL 574]. In the above case, Supreme Court was concerned with an unlisted company. In case of listed companies, the SEBI (ICDR) Regulations, 2009 prohibits issue of bonus shares by capitalization of revaluation reserves. The SEBI (ICDR) Regulations is not applicable to unlisted companies. Thus, under the 1956 Act, an unlisted company could use revaluation reserve for issuing bonus shares.

In order to overcome Supreme Court's decision in Bhagwati Developers (supra), section 63 of 2013 Act provides that no issue of bonus shares shall be made by capitalizing reserves created by the revaluation of assets. This bar on issuing bonus shares out of revaluation reserves applies to all companies whether listed or unlisted.

Under the 2013 Act provides that if company redeems any redeemable preference shares, notice has to be given to ROC with an altered memorandum. This was not required under the 1956 Act.

Therefore, assessee was holding 74.9% shares of TGL immediately before the reduction of capital and also immediately after the reduction of capital. Such capital has been reduced not only in the case of assessee by TGL but the same has been reduced for all the shareholders of the TGL. Though under the concept of joint stock company, the joint stock company is having independent legal entity but for all practical purposes the company is always owned by the shareholders. Therefore, sum total of 100% shareholders would own the net assets of the company. Now let us say a company started with a capital of Rs. 100/- and had assets of Rs. 100/-, then 75% shareholders would own 75% of such assets i.e. Rs. 75. If after few years, this company suffers a loss and the assets are reduced to Rs. 50, then share of the assessee in the assets of the company would be only Rs. 37.50. If the capital of the company is reduced by 50%, even then the share of the assessee would be 75% and it would remain same at Rs. 37.50. Therefore, the effective share of assessee, in the assets of the company, would remain the same immediately before and after reduction of such capital. In other words, the loss suffered by the company would belong to the company and that cannot be allowed to be set off in the hands of the assessee. This position is further supported by another example. If, in the above illustration, after few years, instead of assets becoming Rs. 50/-, it increases to Rs. 200/-, because of profit, and in turn this company issued bonus shares, even then the profit would remain in the books of the company and mere allotment of such bonus shares cannot be subjected to tax. This position was accepted even by the Ld. Counsel of the assessee. Therefore, when the profits of the company which have been distributed to the shareholders by way of bonus shares cannot be assessed, on the same principle losses of the company which have been adjusted by reducing the capital cannot be allowed.

9. We have also perused the decision of the Madras High Court in G. Narasimhan’s case (supra) on which reliance was placed by the revenue. In that case the controversy was whether there was any transfer, exchange or relinquishment involved in reduction of capital for the purposes of capital gains tax under the Act. The Madras High Court held that in reduction of capital, it cannot be said that there was a transfer of a capital asset nor can it be said that there had been any extinguishment of the rights of the shareholder as all the rights of the shareholder as a shareholder continued and remained. This view of the Madras High Court is, however, no more valid in view of the decision of the Supreme Court in Kartikeya V. Sarabhai v. CIT [1997] 228 ITR 163/ 94 Taxman 164 wherein, it has been held that reduction of the right in the capital asset would clearly amount to a transfer within the meaning of that expression in section 2(47) of the Act. The Supreme Court, in the above case, observed :—

". . . While it is no doubt true that the appellant continues to remain a shareholder of the company even with the reduction of share capital, it is not possible to accept the contention that there has been no extinguishment of any part of his right as a shareholder qua the company. It is not necessary for a capital gain to arise that there must be a sale of a capital asset. Sale is only one of the modes of transfer envisaged by section 2(47) of the Act. Relinquishment of the asset or the extinguishment of any right in it, which may not amount to a sale, can also be considered as a transfer . . ." (p. 168)

HELD: As soon as the resolution was passed capitalising the reserves, such reserves became capital and could not afterwards be dealt with by the company as income; and subsequently, when the capital was reduced, - which was in the next year, - and part of the proceeds of the capitalised reserves was handed back to the shareholders, that part could only be handed back in the form in which it existed, namely, capital. The ITO, when he said that the whole transaction was illusory, apparently meant that the real motive of the directors in putting forward those various resolutions, and of the shareholders in passing them, was not to increase the capital for any commercial purposes of the Company, but to increase the capital in order that the subsequent distribution among the shareholders of the reserve funds might be in the form of capital and not of income; but the High Court could not go into the question of what was at the back of the mind of the directors or the shareholders.

It was not competent to the Income-tax authorities to go behind the order confirming the reduction of capital made by the District Court and to hold that what was sought to be released and reduced by the Resolution passed by the Company ‘R’ for reduction of its Share Capital was release of profits and not Share Capital.

If the second condition had not been introduced, bonus shares issued credited as fully paid up would have been liable to be regarded as "dividend" within section 2(6A)(a) but the legislature obviously did not want to tax such bonus shares as dividend and it, therefore, introduced the second condition in section 2(6A)(a) of the 1922 Act. When accumulated profits are capitalized and redeemable preference shares are issued as bonus shares credited as fully paid-up, the capitalized accumulated profits are converted into preference share capital. The balance-sheet thereafter shows the profit and loss account or reserves at a reduced figure and the issued capital at a correspondingly increased figure, the only effect being that one item on the liabilities side of the balance-sheet becomes replaced in whole or part by another item, namely, preference share capital, while the assets side of the balance-sheet remains unaffected. Now it is a fundamental principle of company law that the capital of a company must be maintained intact, for the company being a mere abstraction of law distinct from its members and the liability of the members being limited, it is the capital of the company which provides a minimum safeguard to third parties dealing with the company and the law, therefore, requires that no part of the capital shall be returned to the shareholders except under certain circumstances and by following a certain procedure requiring the scrutiny of the Court and, it is only if the Court sanctions, that there can be repayment to the shareholders in reduction of the capital. But notwithstanding this fundamental principle of maintenance of capital, redeemable preference shares can be repaid in accordance with the terms of issue otherwise than on a formal reduction of capital approved by the Court. The preference share capital collected from the holders of redeemable preference shares or credited as fully paid up out of capitalised accumulated profits can be returned to the shareholders without going through the procedure of reduction of capital, though such return of preference share capital would amount to reduction of capital. This would appear to constitute a departure from the fundamental principle of maintenance of capital, but if one look at section 105B of the Indian Companies Act, 1913, which was the section which governed redemption at the time when the redeemable preference shares in the present case were redeemed, it is found that the purity of this principle is not only not violated but is, on the contrary, preserved in effect, if not in name, by the stringent provisions contained in the section. Redeemable preference shares, according to these provisions, can be repaid out of profits or out of the proceeds of a fresh issue of shares made for the purpose of redemption or out of sale proceeds of any property of the company. If they are redeemed out of the proceeds of a fresh issue, the capital raised on that issue will obviously replace the capital redeemed and, consequently, the capital of the company will be maintained at the original yardstick. If on the other hand they are redeemed out of profits or out of sale proceeds of any property of the company, then out of profits an amount equivalent to the nominal amount of the shares redeemed is required to be transferred to a reserve fund to be called "The capital redemption reserve fund" which is to be treated as equivalent to paid up capital. Hence, although the redeemable preference shares disappear on redemption, the capital which they represent is retained for accounting purposes and there is no reduction of the capital yardstick. This analysis of the mechanics of redemption clearly shows that when redeemable preference shares are redeemed, the preference share capital is returned to the shareholders and since such return of the preference share capital would deplete the capital of the company and consequently affect the sanctity of the principle of maintenance of capital which is regarded as a principle of paramount importance, the law requires that the preference share capital so returned should be replaced by other capital either provided by a fresh issue of shares made for the purpose of redemption or transferred out of the profits of the company in case redemption is made out of profits or out of sale proceeds of any property of the company. It is undoubtedly true that redemption cannot be made except out of profits of the company or out of proceeds of a fresh issue of shares made for the purpose of redemption or out of sale proceeds of any property of the company, but these merely indicate the sources of the moneys which may be utilised for the purpose of returning the preference share capital to the shareholders. The only inhibition is that if a company wants to return the preference share capital to the shareholders the company must do so out of moneys earned by the company as profits or derived by the company from a fresh issue of shares or obtained by the company by selling any property belonging to it and if there are no such moneys, the company cannot return the preference share capital to its shareholders. But what is returned to the shareholders on redemption, what is distributed amongst them, is the preference share capital and not the profits of the company, or proceeds of the fresh issue of shares made for the purpose of redemption or sale proceeds of the property belonging to the company which merely provide the moneys for return of the preference share capital.
