WHETHER BONUS SHARES CAN BE ISSUED OUT OF REVALUATION RESERVE - THE CONTROVERSY

5. Before the abolition of the Capital Issues (Control) Act, 1947, the Controller of Capital Issues had categorically stated in his guidelines for issue of bonus shares that reserves created by revaluation of fixed assets are not permitted to be capitalized. The Department of Company Affairs has issued Circular No. 9 of 1994 dated September 6, 1994 prohibiting issue of bonus shares out of revaluation reserves. The text of the circular is given below:

"Prohibition of issue of bonus shares out of reserves created by revaluation of fixed assets

I am directed to say that...it has come to the notice of the Department that a number of unlisted companies (existing private/closely held public companies) are resorting to revaluation of their assets and issuing bonus shares therefrom. The latest Securities and Exchange Board of India’s guidelines on bonus shares dated April 13, 1994, inter alia, stipulate that the bonus issue has to be made out of free reserves built out of the genuine profits or share premium collected in cash only and reserves created by revaluation of fixed assets cannot be capitalized for this purpose. These guidelines are applicable only to listed companies.

This matter has been considered in the Department and the existing private/closely held and unlisted companies are hereby advised not to issue bonus shares out of the reserves created by revaluation of fixed assets."

SOME OBSERVATIONS ON THE ABOVE CIRCULAR

6. There is no provision in the Companies Act, 1956 dealing with the kind of reserve which may be used for the purpose of issue of bonus share except for an enabling provision under proviso to section 205(3) which enables the company to capitalize profits or ‘reserves’ for the purpose of issuing bonus shares. The term ‘reserve’ is negatively defined in Schedule VI, Part III: the expression ‘reserve’ shall not include the amount written of or retained by way of providing for depreciation, renewals or diminution in the value of assets or retained by way of providing for known liability. Revaluation Reserve therefore, cannot be excluded in terms of this definition from being termed as Reserve.

POSITION UNDER ENGLISH LAW

7. The permissibility of capitalizing Revaluation Reserve is judicially recognized in England. This is clear from the authority of the decision in Dimbulla Valley (Ceylon) Tea Co. Ltd. v. Laurie [1961] 1 Ch 353 in which the eminent Judge BUCKLEY J. observed as follows: "It has, I think, long been generally accepted view of the law in this country. (Though not established by judicial authority) that if the surplus on capital account results from a valuation made in good faith by competent valuers, and is not likely to be liable to short term fluctuations, it may properly be capitalised."

SEBI DOES NOT PROHIBIT BONUS OUT OF REVALUATION RESERVE BY UNLISTED COMPANIES

8. SEBI have in the DIP Guidelines recognized the legal position that an unlisted company can issue bonus shares by capitalizing its Revaluation Reserves. This is brought out by clause 4.6.1(ii) of the SEBI (Disclosure & Investor Protection) Guidelines, 2000 (‘the DIP Guidelines) which deal with promoters contribution. Clause 4.6 of the DIP Guidelines reads as under:

"4.6 Securities Ineligible for Computation of Promoters Contribution.

4.6.1 Where the promoters of any company making an issue of securities have acquired equity during the preceding three years, before filing the offer documents with the Board, such equity shall not be considered for computation of promoters contribution if it is:

"(i) acquired for consideration other than cash and revaluation of assets or capitalization of intangible assets is involved in such transaction(s) ; or

(ii) resulting from a bonus issues, out of revaluation reserves or reserves without accrual of cash resources."

Per Chhibber, Accountant Member - This appeal by the assessee is directed against the order of the CIT (Appeals)-I, Pune.

2. The assessee is an Investment Company floated by Kalyani group. During the year under appeal, it has shown property income, income from business and capital gain on the sale of shares of Bharat Forge Ltd. and also income on account of dealing in the shares of other companies.

3. The first grievance of the assessee is with regard to the computation of capital gains on the sale of shares and bonus shares. The assessee had acquired 68740 shares of M/s. Bharat Forge Ltd. in 1977 on the dissolution of the firm M/s. Kalyani Brothers, wherein it was a partner. On 20-6-1981, it got bonus shares in the ratio of 1:1, i.e., 68740. Again it got 1780 Bonus shares in 1989. It retained these shares as stock-in-trade in its Balance sheet till 30-6-1988 and on 1-7-1988, these shares were converted into capital asset at the rate of Rs. 17 per share. Out of these shares, during this year, the assessee sold 68740 shares on which capital gains were shown. While working out the capital gains, the assessee adopted the fair market value as on 1-4-1981 as per the provisions of section 55(2)(b). The Assessing Officer held that the assessee was not entitled to exercise this option because as on that date, these shares were held by the assessee as stock-in-trade and not as capital assets. According to the Assessing Officer, capital asset does not include stock-in-trade as per section 2(14). Since the shares were treated as stock-in-trade by the assessee upto 30-6-1988, it cannot be said that there was any capital asset in existence prior to this date. Therefore, for the purpose of computing long term capital gain, the first year of acquisition of capital asset has to be taken as financial year 1988-89. Since the capital asset has come into existence only on 1-7-1988, the market value of these shares as on 1-4-1981 cannot be adopted as provided under section 55(2)(3) of the Income-tax Act, 1961. Secondly, while computing the cost of acquisition of bonus shares, the assessee had computed the same by spreading over the indexed cost of acquisition upto the date of issue of bonus shares and not cost of acquisition. According to the Assessing Officer, this was not correct and the indexed cost of acquisition is to be computed from the cost of acquisition. The cost of acquisition of bonus shares has to be computed by spreading over the cost of acquisition of original assets over the original assets and bonus shares issued, as decided by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Escorts Farms (Ramgarh) Ltd. v. CIT [1996] 222 ITR 5091 . The indexed cost of acquisition is, therefore, to be computed from the cost of acquisition and not by spreading the indexed cost of acquisition of original holding. The Assessing Officer accordingly computed the capital gains as per Annexure to the assessment order, which was challenged before the CIT (Appeals).

distribution must be such as entails release of assets of the company and if, therefore, the distribution does not entail release of assets of the company, though the first condition would be satisfied, the second would not be and the distribution would not, therefore, be dividend within section 2(6A)(a) 1922 Act. Now admittedly there was release of assets of the company on redemption since moneys were actually paid out of the coffers of the company and received by the shareholders. A company must state in its memorandum of association the amount of capital with which the company desires to do business and the number of shares into which that capital is to be divided. The company need not issue all its capital at one time. It may issue only a part of its capital initially and issue the rest of the unissued capital or a part of it at a later date. Now if a company prospers and earns profits it may do one of two things with the profits. It may either distribute the profits by way of dividend among the shareholders or accumulate them. Generally, when a company accumulates profits it carries them to various reserves which appear on the liabilities side of the balance-sheet. Ordinarily, these undistributed profits are employed in the business either in acquisition of fixed assets or as working capital and really represent an increase in the capital employed in the business. When these increase to a considerable extent, the issued capital of the company ceases to bear a true relation to the real capital employed in the business. The company may, in such a case, decide to bring its issued capital into a truer relationship with the capital actually employed in the business or, to use the words of Gower, "more into line with the true excess of assets over liabilities" and may for that purpose capitalise its accumulated profits and issue fully paid up bonus shares of a nominal value equal to the amount capitalised to its shareholders. These bonus shares may be either ordinary or preference shares on the one hand or redeemable preference shares on the other. The company may also instead of issuing bonus shares issue bonus debentures by capitalising its accumulated profits. In all these cases the accumulated profits which are capitalised remain in the coffers of the company and no part of them actually goes into the pockets of the shareholders : the only change that takes place is that the accumulated profits which prior to capitalisation were employed in the business as accumulated profits are thenceforth employed as part of the issued or loan capital of the company according as the issue is of bonus shares or bonus debentures. The accumulated profits which might have been divided among the shareholders as dividend are impounded to increase the capital of the company and what the shareholders get is not any payment out of the accumulated profits but bonus shares or bonus debentures credited as fully paid up. The transaction, to use the words of Viscount Cave in Commissioners of Inland Revenue v. John Blott [1921] 8 Tax Cas. 101, 135, takes "nothing out of the company’s coffers and "puts" nothing into the shareholders’ pockets" but what happens is that the accumulated profits which are capitalized are applied in paying up the amounts due on bonus shares or debentures to be issued to the shareholders as fully paid up bonus shares or debentures. This analysis of the mechanism of issue of bonus shares or debentures is, apart from the abundance of authority to support it, clearly based on sound principle. It is clear law that when shares are issued and allotted by a company the liability for the amount due on the shares is always on the allottee and that liability must be satisfied from some source external to the company in money or money’s worth. The allottee may pay the amount due on the shares in money or money’s worth. The allottee may pay the amount due on the shares in money or if the allottee has to his credit any amount due by the company, such credit may, with his consent, be applied in discharge of the allottee's liabilities on the shares. Now admittedly no moneys are paid by the shareholders for the bonus shares issued to them and it must, therefore, follow that when bonus shares are issued credited as fully paid up, the liability for payment in full on allotment which the shareholders would otherwise have had to discharge is paid by the company by applying the accumulated profits to the discharge of such liability for the benefit of the shareholders. There is of course no payment of the accumulated profits to the shareholders since no part of the accumulated profits is liberated to them: the company does not part with any of the accumulated profits nor do the shareholders receive any part of them. But the accumulated profits are applied in paying up the capital sums which the shareholders would otherwise have had to contribute for the purpose of new shares. The shareholders receiving bonus shares credited as fully paid up are given credit for the capital sums which they would otherwise have had to contribute in respect of the bonus shares allotted to them if those shares had not been issued credited as fully paid up and this credit is given by application of the capitalised accumulated profits in payment of such capital sums. As observed by Hidayatullah J. in CIT v. Dalmia Investment Co. Ltd [1964] 52 ITR 567 (SC), after the accumulated profits are converted into capital and bonus shares are issued credited as fully paid up "the company employs that money not as reserves of profits, but as its proper capital issued to and contributed by the shareholder"

The term 'dividend' has been defined under section 2(22)(a) and as per said definition, any distribution by a company to its shareholders to the extent of accumulated profits, whether capitalized or not, such distribution entails the release by the company to its shareholders of all or any part of the assets of the company. The definition is an inclusive definition and it goes beyond the conventional or traditional meaning associated with dividend. The definition is broad and covers a wide variety of payments made by a company. In fact, section 2(22)(e) even includes a loan given by a company to its shareholder, subject to certain conditions, within the ambit of dividend. Therefore, the object of such an expansive definition seems to be ensure that the taxpayer do not camouflage payments out of accumulates profits to its shareholders through different channels in order to avoid payment of tax. Section 2(22)(a) covers any distribution by a company of accumulated profits which entails the release by the company to its shareholders of all or any of the assets of the company. Section 2(22)(d) covers distribution made to the shareholders by a company on the reduction of its share capital to the extent the company possess accumulated profits. Two essential pre-requisites must be satisfied in order to come within the ambit of section 2(22)(d) i.e., there must be a distribution to the shareholders on the reduction of the capital and further, it must be to the extent that the company possess accumulated profits. In the instant case, which is evident from the audited financial statement that the share capital has been reduced by around Rs. 9.4 Crs. which is equivalent to 54.70 per cent of the total paid up share capital. Further, Clause 7 of the scheme makes it clear that the distribution of money will be out of the general reserves and accumulated credit balance in the profit and loss account. Thus, both conditions are satisfied to treat the transaction within the ambit of section 2(22)(d). [Para 34]

The Company Court exercises jurisdiction which was founded on fairness. While exercising its jurisdiction, the Court was competent to examine the bona fides or fairness of the valuation of shares or the exchange ratio and whether the proposal conforms to commercial morality. It was held that having regard to the litigation history in the transferee company involving the objector and other related developments and also having regard to the financial status of the transferor company as discussed above, objection raised by the objector and by the Central Government through the Regional Director regarding the exchange ratio of shares between the two companies could not be brushed aside. Accordingly, the Registrar of Companies was directed to work out the exchange ratio in a fair manner through independent experts keeping in view the discussions made and were asked to submit the same to the Court in two months time. 2. Heritage Housing Finance Ltd., Inre [2013] 40 taxmann.com 103/[2014] 124 SCL 319 (Cal.)

Similar to the case discussed above was the case of "Heritage Housing Finance Ltd" wherein the Central Government raised an objection that the share exchange ratio as proposed in the said scheme was not fair and reasonable. The petitioner filed petition contending that the Central Government could not raise aforesaid objection when in the shareholders' meeting the entire scheme had been approved unanimously. It was held that the plain reading of the provisions did not postulate the nature of the objection required to be raised by the Central Government but what it provided was that the Court before passing any order ,must take into consideration the representations and/or objections raised by the Central Government. It was held that the Central Government was certainly within their competence to raise the objection as they were required to see that no unfairness and/or unreasonableness to be shown either to the creditors or the class of creditors and/or members or the class of members and public interest, which certainly imbibed itself with the power to question the said share exchange ratio. Therefore, there was no force in the submission of the petitioner that the Central Government could not raise objection to the share exchange ratio. It was therefore directed to the official liquidator to engage a Chartered Accountant from its panel, who should submit the report before the court relating to fairness of the share exchange ratio.

of acquisition for the purpose of determination of capital gains and the statutory right cannot be taken away by limiting the scope of section 49(2) and treating the shares held in the amalgamated company as a new asset. The intention of the Parliament is to reduce the tax liability in the case of amalgamation and it is clear that under the provisions of section 49(2), the cost of the shares shall be deemed to be the cost of acquisition of shares in the amalgamating company. Once it is held that there is no change in the ownership, the assessee is entitled to exercise his statutory option to substitute the market value of shares of the amalgamating company as on 1-1-1964, as the cost of the shares under section 55(2)(i). Section 49(2) is extended to determine the cost of acquisition of shares of the amalgamated company but that does not take away the right of the assessee to exercise his option under section 55(2)(i) in adopting the market value of the shares of the amalgamated company as on 1-1-1964. By virtue of section 49(2), the cost of the shares in the amalgamated company is deemed to be the cost of the shares in the amalgamating company and when the shares held by him in the amalgamated company were sold, the assessee had an option to take either the actual cost of the asset or the fair market value of the asset as on 1-1-1964. Therefore, the non-availability of an option under section 55(2)(ii ) does not prevent the exercise of the option provided under section 55(2)(i ). The expression ‘cost of acquisition’ found in sections 48, 49 and 55 is a compendious expression and in the context of levy of capital gains, the general principle of law relating to the cost determination of acquisition cannot be imported. Section 49(2) does not postulate the manner in which the cost of acquisition of shares in two amalgamating companies should be calculated. It merely declares that the cost of acquisition of the shares in the amalgamated company shall be deemed to be the cost of acquisition to him of the shares held in the amalgamating company. The cost of acquisition of shares held in the amalgamated company would be relevant at the time of transfer of the shares held by the assessee in the amalgamated company in the context of levy of capital gains and, at that point of time, when the cost of acquisition of shares in the amalgamating company has to be determined, the assessee has an option either to adopt the actual cost of acquisition of shares in the amalgamating company or to adopt the fair market value of the shares as on 1-1-1964. The statutory right is not taken away by section 55(2)(ii) as the right is available to him under section 55(2)(i). It is not possible to give a restricted meaning to the expression found in section 49(2) that the cost of shares shall be deemed to be the cost of acquisition of shares in the amalgamating company and that figure is an unalterable figure. Section 49(2) and section 55(2)(i) should be read together.

The principle laid down by the Bombay High Court in Harish Mahindra v. CIT [1982] 135 ITR 191/[1981] 7 Taxman 301, would apply to a case of transfer of shares held in the amalgamated company allotted in lieu of shares in the amalgamating company and the assessee was entitled to exercise the option under section 55(2)(i) as his original shares were acquired prior to 1-1-1964. Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) and the Tribunal committed no error in holding that the assessee was entitled to exercise the option under section 55(2)(i).

However, once the fair market value of the shares as on 1-1-1964 was determined, it remained on unalterable figure and any issue of bonus shares subsequent to that date was wholly extraneous and irrelevant and could not be taken into consideration. Therefore, when all the shares including bonus shares were sold and transferred, it was not necessary to ascertain the value of bonus shares separately and the cost of all shares being a known figure, it would be deducted to compute the capital gains. The view arrived at by the Tribunal was in consonance with various decisions. Accordingly, there was no infirmity in the order of the Tribunal in holding that the assessee was not entitled to deduction the cost of bonus shares in addition to the cost of acquisition of original shares in the two amalgamated companies.

Pointers for tax planning 12. From the tax planning angle, the following aspects may have to be kept in view:

(i) In view of the substantial difference between the rate of tax applicable to long-term capital gains (10%), and the rate applicable to short-term capital gain (30%), it is desirable to hold on to the specified securities for a minimum period of 12 months before contemplating to transfer them.

Some areas of doubt

13. In the interpretation of section 115AD of the Act, doubts are bound to arise in quite a few areas. Two such areas of doubt are dealt with below:

(i) In the case of renunciation of rights offer for a consideration, a doubt may arise whether the resulting gain will fall within the purview of section 115AD of the Act. The extreme view that could possibly be taken is that such gain cannot be treated as "income received in respect of securities", nor as "income by way of short-term capital gain", with the result that the rates prescribed in section 115AD of the Act cannot be applied. While there cannot be any doubt that such gain cannot be treated as "income by way of capital gain" as contemplated in section 115AD of the Act, there is no reason why it cannot be treated as "income received in respect of securities" as envisaged in that provision. In Union of India v. Vijay Chand Jain [1977] 47 Comp. Cas. 674, the Supreme Court observed that the expression "in respect of" in its widest sense, means "connected with". Undoubtedly, the rights offer is connected with the holding of the specified securities, and hence any gain arising by its exploitation can be construed as "income received in respect of securities".

(ii ) Another area of doubt that may arise is about the applicability of section 115AD of the Act to a FII who is a dealer in shares and securities, and not an investor. The question that would arise in such a case is whether the profits arising to a FII from the business of dealing in shares and securities can be treated as "income in respect of securities" as envisaged in section 115AD of the Act. One line of thinking is that such profits not per se arise from the securities, but they arise from the business of dealing in securities, and hence the concessional rate of 20 per cent cannot be applied. With due respect, the author bags to differ from this view. The clue to the problem can be found in the wordings of section 115AD themselves. It states, inter alia, that in the computation of income received in respect of the securities, no deductions under sections 28 to 44C will be allowed. These provisions in the Act deal with the deductions available in the computation of business income. If an embargo has been placed on such deductions, it is simply a matter of inference to conclude that even if the income becomes classifiable as business income, the benefits conferred under section 115AD of the Act cannot be denied. Otherwise, the use of the expression "sections 28 to 44C" in section 115AD will be rendered meaningless. The Legislature cannot be imputed with wasting words in a statutory provision, and from the very fact that the Legislature has placed an embargo on allowing deductions under sections 28 to 44C, it is a logical presumption that it was not the intention of Legislature to deny the benefit of concessional rates to a FII who is a dealer in shares and securities.

12. The Supreme Court has held in Bhagwati Developers v. Peerless General Finance & Investment Co. [2005] 62 SCL 574 that unlisted public companies can issue bonus shares out of revaluation reserve.

12.1 FACTUAL MATRIX - The facts of the case are:

The respondent-company issued bonus shares for Rs. 31 crores out of Rs. 73 crores standing in revaluation reserve. The appellant, who was a shareholder of the company, filed a suit against the respondent for a declaration that it was not entitled to issue bonus shares out of revaluation reserve. The appellant challenged the power of the respondent-company to issue bonus shares out of revaluation reserve on three grounds. viz., (a) that the bonus shares had been issued contrary to SEBI guidelines, (b) that the issue was contrary to the circular issued by the Department of Company Affairs; and (c) that the issue could not have been made as it was contrary to article 182 of the articles of association of the company. The Calcutta High Court, in its impugned order, held that the respondent-company was entitled to issue bonus shares out of revaluation reserve. The shareholder preferred an appeal against the High Court’s order to the Apex Court.

12.2 JUDGMENT - SEBI has clarified on August 13, 1992 that its guidelines do not apply to issue of securities by closely-held private companies and unlisted public companies. (Para 6)

The circular dated September 6, 1994 does not have any mandatory effect. These circulars are merely advisory in character. (Para 7)

The relevant portion of the article 182 of the articles of association of the company, which had been strongly relied upon reads as follows :

"182(1) Any General Meeting may resolve that any amounts standing to the credit of the share premium account or the capital redemption reserve account or any monies, investment or other assets forming part of the undivided profits including profits or surplus monies arising from the realization and (where permitted by law from the appreciation in value of any capital assets of the company) standing to the credit of the General Reserve, or any Reserve Fund or any other fund of the company or in the hands of the company and available for dividend be capitalized:

(i) by the issue and distribution as fully paid-up shares, debentures, debenture stock, bonds or other obligations of the company, or

Issuing bonus shares out of revaluation reserve 6.1 Existing prohibition - Section M of the SEBI Guidelines for Disclosure and Investor Protection does not allow issue of bonus shares out of the Revaluation reserve. This prohibition is applicable to listed companies. The Department of Company Affairs vide its Circular No. 9/94 (Circular Letter No. 17/32/93 - CL V dated September 6,1994) has also prohibited issue of bonus shares out of revaluation reserve by the existing private/ closely-held and unlisted companies.

The Guidance note on availability of revaluation reserve for issue of bonus shares issued by the ICAI (Published in November 1994 issue of the Chartered Accountant) argues that the excess of the revalued amount over the net book value of fixed assets, which is credited to revaluation reserve, is created as a result of book adjustment only. The revaluation reserve does not result from an arm's length transaction; it represents an expert's perception of value. The revaluation reserve thus does not represent realised gain.

The ICAI Guidance Note also states that share capital represents money or money's worth received from the owners and capitalisation of earned profits or other gains arising out of arm's length transactions. It is a cardinal principle that only such profits as are earned or the relevant capital receipts (e.g. share premium) as are realised, can be capitalised.

6.2 Expert's value perception - So long as the expert's perception of the fair value of a fixed asset is judicious, there is nothing wrong in depending on such valuation, in case the upper limit of revaluation is restricted to the net recoverable amount. Substitution of historical cost becomes necessary when it materially differs from the fair value of the fixed assets. A going concern may not think of disposing of a particular asset, still the increase in value of the asset, although unrealised, cannot be denied. Since the revaluation reserve forms part of the shareholders' funds, it should be treated as a free reserve.

6.3 Arm's length transactions and business income -The concept of arm's length relationship is altogether irrelevant in this context. The reported net profit of an entity is not necessarily the result of arm's length transactions. Also it is not necessary for the purpose of a bonus issue to consider to what extent the accumulated surplus of the entity has resulted from arm's length transactions.

6.4 Unrealised gain - Of course, the revaluation reserve represents unrealised gain. But it represents real gain and cannot be treated as a fictitious gain. Accordingly, the shareholders should not be denied the right to utilise any such real gain in the manner they want. It is not unknown to the shareholders that such a bonus issue, if any, results from unrealised gain.

6.5 Accounting effect of bonus issue - Presently, many companies take a transfer from the revaluation reserve to the extent of additional depreciation. To that extent profit is inflated every year and the revaluation reserve is converted into the so called 'earned profit'. It is just a matter of time to convert revaluation reserve into 'earned profit' and as soon as the conversion is complete there is no bar on utilising such 'earned profit' for issuing bonus shares.

In case the revaluation reserve is utilised for a bonus issue, the company would have no choice but to charge additional depreciation out of profit.

6.6 Corporate freedom - One of the basic tenets of economic liberalisation is reduction/elimination of bureaucratic interference on the activities of private entrepreneurs. Corporate management should be given freedom to adopt a suitable financial management policy. A bonus issue out of the revaluation reserve will not generally be supported by increase in the earning capacity. However, the management will not find difficulty in maintaining the dividend rate in real terms. A decline in post-equity pricewill have no effect in real terms, since this book adjustment has no effect on the earnings of the entity.

12. Cognizant liable to pay DDT on its Rs. 19,000 crores buyback: ITAT [Cognizant Technology Solutions India (P.) Ltd. v. Asst. CIT [2023] 154 taxmann.com 309 (Chennai - Trib.)]

The assessee (Cognizant Technology) had purchased its own shares from non-resident shareholders in a 'Scheme of Arrangement & Compromise' sanctioned by the High Court of Madras in terms of provisions of Section 391-393 of the Companies Act, 1956.

In accordance with the scheme, the assessee purchased 94,00,534 equity shares from its shareholder at the price of Rs. 20,297 per share and paid a total consideration of Rs. 19,080.26 crores.

The share capital of the assessee company was held by four non-resident shareholders, out of which three shareholders are residents of the USA, and one shareholder is a tax resident of Mauritius. The net effect of the scheme was that post-sanction of the scheme, the only shareholder left was Cognizant Mauritius Ltd.

The AO held that consideration paid by the assessee to its shareholders for the purchase of its own shares was liable to tax as deemed dividend under Section 2(22)(d). Consequently, the assessee was liable to pay Dividend Distribution Tax (DDT) under Section 115-O.

On the other hand, the assessee submits that the 'Scheme of Arrangement & Compromise' was sanctioned by the High Court of Madras in terms of Sections 391 to 393 of the Companies Act, 1956. It cannot be considered as a buyback of shares in terms of provisions of Section 77A or a reduction of capital in terms of Sections 100-104/402 of the Companies Act, 1956.

On appeal, the CIT(A) upheld the findings of AO. The matter reached before the tribunal.

The tribunal held as follows:

Two essential prerequisites must be satisfied to come within the ambit of Section 2(22)(d). First, there must be a distribution to the shareholders on the reduction of the capital, and second, it must be to the extent that the company possess accumulated profits. In the present case, it was evident from the audited financial statement that the share capital has been reduced by around Rs. 9.4 crores, which is equivalent to 54.70% of the total paid-up share capital. The Supreme Court, in CIT v. G. Narasihan 236 ITR 327, has clarified that Section 2(22)(d) is automatically attracted once these parameters are satisfied. Further, Clause 7 of the scheme clarifies that the distribution of money will be out of the general reserves and accumulated credit balance in the profit and loss account. Thus, both conditions are satisfied to treat the transaction within Section 2(22)(d).

The assessee also argued that the scheme of purchase of own shares was made through offer and acceptance. This involves an element of quid pro quo, and thus, there was no 'distribution of the purpose of section 2(22)(d). The tribunal held that the definition of 'distribution' does not contain any aspect of quid pro quo or lack thereof. The prerequisites for distribution are that there must be payment, and the disbursal must be made to more than one person. Section 2(22)(d) does not distinguish whether the reduction of share capital is the intended result of the resultant consequence of the scheme.

The assessee's transaction would either fall under Section 391-393 r.w. Section 77 and Section 100 of the Companies Act, 1956 or Sections 391-393 r.w Section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956. The scheme clearly states that it is not a buyback under Section 77A. Therefore, once the assessee states it is not buyback under section 77A, it should automatically fall back to Section 77 r.w Sections 100-104 of the Companies Act, 1956. If said sections are applied, then said transaction was nothing but the reduction of capital and distribution of accumulated profits.

The assessee also contended that Section 115QA was amended in 2016, and the present transaction would only be taxable per the amended provisions. The assessee's arguments were not accepted for two reasons. Firstly, there is a distinction between the purchase of own shares upon reduction of share capital and buyback. Buyback is a term used only with respect to transactions covered under Section 77A. If all conditions of Section 115-O r.w Section 2(22) are satisfied, the same cannot be impliedly excluded based on the amendment to Section 115QA.

The Bombay High Court specifically referred to the observations of the Supreme Court in India Cements Ltd.'s case (supra) at page 61 ‘obtaining capital by issue of shares is different from obtaining loan by debentures’.

15. We also note that the Supreme Court at page 63 had summarized the position by pointing out that the loan obtained is not an asset or advantage of an enduring nature.

However, dealing with expenditure on printing and stationery and postage and telegrams, the High Court observed that the said expenses were incurred consequent upon the issue of bonus shares and they were not expenses which could be said to be incurred for the purpose of raising any additional capital and, therefore, these expenses were incurred in the normal course of the assessee-company’s business. The Bombay High Court accordingly held that the said expenditure was not capital expenditure. We may, however, distinguish our case from the aforesaid case of Bombay Burmah Trading Corpn. Ltd. (supra) where a running company had issued bonus shares and the expenditure on printing and stationery, etc., was incurred in the normal course of business and not for the purpose of raising any additional capital (page 804); while, in our case, the company is going through stages of standing on its feet as an independent entity and not as a subsidiary of a foreign company and the expenses are being incurred on raising its original capital (see page 7 of prospectus). Therefore, the expenditure even on printing and stationery and postage and telegrams does form an integral part of the expenditure incurred on raising the initial capital of the assessee-company.

18. The learned counsel for the assessee relied on the aforesaid decision in Kisenchand Chellaram ( India) ( P.) Ltd.’s case (supra) and urged that the aforesaid expenditure of Rs. 8,07,624 was incurred for continuing the assessee’s business and to comply with the Reserve Bank’s directions for diluting the foreign equity to 40 per cent. As we pointed out to the assessee’s counsel, this could be done by offering 60 per cent of the holding of the foreign shareholders to the public as was done by many FERA companies. The fact remains that the assessee-company was raising its initial share capital from the public and the said expenditure was incurred for raising the said share capital.

V. Revenue's reliance on section 92(2) of the Act a.

Section 92(2) of the Act, deals with a situation where two or more AEs enter into an arrangement whereby they are to receive any benefit, service or facility then the allocation, apportionment or contribution towards the cost or expenditure is to be determined in respect of each AE having regard to the ALP. It would have no application in the taxpayer's case where there is no occasion to allocate, apportion or contribute any cost and/or expenses between the taxpayer and the AE.

VI. Revenue's reliance on section 56 of the Act – Income from other sources

a.

Although section 56(1) of the Act would permit including within its head, all income not otherwise excluded, it does not provide for a charge to tax on capital account transaction of issue of shares as is specifically provided for in section 45 or section 56(2)(viib) of the Act and included within the definition of "income" in section 2(24) of the Act.

CONCLUSION

Issue of shares at a premium by the taxpayer to its AE does not give rise to any "income" from an admitted International Transaction. Therefore, there is no need to invoke TP provisions.

KEY TAKEAWAYS

The judgment delivered by the Bombay HC in favour of the taxpayer saves it from the rigours of the ongoing high pitched TP litigation. It is a welcome judgment as the transaction of issue of shares by the taxpayer was nothing but a capital account transaction, and consequently the share premium, if any, ought to be capital receipt. The decision has made it clear that TP adjustments are also subject to fundamentals of chargeability of income and the TP provisions permit the transaction to be re-quantified but not to be re-characterised. Hence, there was no question of the transaction resulting in "income" taxable in India. The judgment will not only serve as a precedent in the legal arena but will also lend a much needed boost to foreign investors. The judgment brings relief to numerous companies who are saddled with such an unnecessary adjustment. It is timely in the light of our Prime Minister's invitation to the world to manufacture and invest in India. This will certainly help in boosting the "Make in India" campaign and the overall investment climate of the country.

5. ARGUMENTS BEFORE THE HIGH COURT 6. HIGH COURT'S VERDICT

The Bombay High Court held that on the facts of the present case, issue of shares at a premium by VISL to its non-resident AE does not give rise to any income from an admitted international transaction and thus, Indian Transfer Pricing provisions are not applicable for the following reasons:

Income arising from an international transaction is a pre-condition for application of Transfer Pricing provisions. Further, the Act defines the term income in an inclusive manner. Income, in its normal meaning, will not include capital receipts unless specifically provided. The amounts received on issue of share capital including the premium are on capital account. In this case, what is being sought to be taxed is capital forgone i.e. not received from a non-resident in the form of short premium. Therefore, absent express legislation, an amount received, accrued or arising on capital account transactions cannot be subjected to tax as income.

The High Court further held that the transaction on capital account or on account of restructuring would become taxable to the extent it impacts income i.e., under-reporting of interest received/over reporting of interest paid or claiming of depreciation. It is that income (and not the capital receipt) which is to be determined having regard to the ALP under the Transfer Pricing provisions.

The Transfer Pricing provisions are brought into statute books to ensure that the transaction is taxed only on the income computed as per the ALP of the transaction and to ensure that there is no manipulation of prices/consideration between AEs.

In any case, the entire exercise of taxing the amounts allegedly not received as share premium fails, as no tax is charged on the amount received as share premium.

Neither the capital receipts received by VISL on issue of equity shares to its AE nor the shortfall between the alleged FMV of its equity shares and the issue price of the equity shares can be considered as income within the meaning of the expression as defined in the Act and hence not subject to Transfer Pricing provisions in India.

The reasoning that if the ALP were received, the Taxpayer would be able to invest the same and earn income, proceeds on a mere surmise/assumption and that this cannot be the basis of taxation.

The Tax Authorities relied on this section to argue that differences between the ALP and the price charged for issue of shares is the benefit conferred upon the holding company.

Relying on section 92(2) of the Act is misplaced. Section 92(2) of the Act, which deals with a situation where two or more AEs enter into an arrangement whereby they are to receive any benefit, service or facility then the allocation, apportionment or contribution of the corresponding cost or expenditure is to be determined for each AE based on ALP, is meant to cover cases of cost sharing arrangements and/or cost contribution arrangements. Section 92(2) would have no application in cases like the present one, where there is no occasion to allocate, apportion or contribute any cost and/or expenses between the Taxpayer and its AE. Ignoring words in a statute to achieve a predetermined objective is not permissible and the same would amount to re-drafting the legislation, which is beyond the jurisdiction of the Courts.

The contention of the Tax Authorities that in view of the Transfer Pricing provisions, notional income is to be taxed and real income is not relevant is unacceptable. The entire exercise of determining the ALP is only to arrive at the real income earned.

Even income arising from international transactions between AEs must satisfy the test of income per se under the Act and must find its home under one of the charging provisions. It is a re-computation exercise to be carried out only when income arises in case of an international transaction between AEs. It does not warrant recomputation of a consideration received/given on capital account except in cases of interest paid/received on loans taken/given, depreciation taken on machinery, etc. Therefore, in the absence of a charging provision to tax issue of shares at a premium to a non-resident, the occasion to invoke the computational Transfer Pricing provisions does not arise.

Further, in view of inclusion of issue of shares, by a company to another resident, at a price in excess of FMV in the definition of income under the Act, there is conscious intention of the Parliament to not tax amounts received from a non-resident for issue of shares, as it would discourage capital inflow from abroad.

7. CONCLUSION

In the backdrop of the present Government's initiative to bring in foreign investment, this decision from the Bombay High Court's is a landmark. The High Court has been rightly able to distinguish between the 'income' per se and the capital which is primarily the source to earn income. One important take away from the decision is the High Court's acknowledgement that mere reporting of an international transaction out of abundant caution would not make the same taxable if there is no income arising from such international transaction.

In the case of shares, however, the cost of acquisition will have to be determined in the following manner:

Original shares: Where the shares are acquired in a public offer or from the stock market, the cost of acquisition will be the amount actually paid for acquiring the shares, again without the benefit of indexation.

Right shares: Where the assessee acquires the shares offered on right basis, the cost of acquisition will be the amount actually paid by the assessee for acquiring the shares. Where the assessee renounces the rights offer in favour of another person (the renouncee), and the renouncee acquires the shares, the cost of acquisition of such shares to the renouncee will be the sum total of the consideration paid to the renouncer and the amount paid to the company allotting the rights share.

Rights entitlement: Where the assessee-shareholder renounces the right offer (either in whole or in part) for a consideration in favour of a third party, the cost of acquisition of the rights entitlement will, under section 55(2)(aa) of the Act inserted with effect from 1-4-1995, be taken as nil. In other words, the entire consideration received by the renouncer-assessee will be treated as capital gain.

Bonus shares: In reality, a shareholder does not incur any "cost" in respect of bonus shares. However, in a series of decisions, the Supreme Court had held that the correct method for ascertaining the cost of bonus shares which rank pari passu with the original shares will be to take the amount spent by the shareholder in acquiring the original shares and to spread it over the old and new shares. In other words, the cost of bonus shares will have to be determined by treating the old cost price of the original shares as the cost price of the old shares and bonus shares taken together. Reference in this regard may be made to the decisions of the Supreme Court in the cases of CIT v. Dalmia Investment Co. Ltd. [1964] 52 ITR 567, CIT v. Gold Mohore Investment Co. Ltd. [1968] 68 ITR 213 and CIT v. Gold Co. Ltd. [1970] 78 ITR 16.

Illustration: Suppose a FII purchased 4000 shares in a company in the year 1993 at a price of Rs. 125 per share, and the company issued bonus shares in the ratio of 1:2 in the year 1994. The FII would have received 2000 bonus shares. The cost of acquisition of these bonus shares will work out to - (4000 × 125) divided by 6000, i.e., Rs. 83.33 per bonus share.

Deductions under Chapter VI-A not allowable

11. Chapter VI-A of the Act, comprising sections 80A to 80VV, grants certain deductions by way of incentives. Section 115AD of the Act stipulates that these deductions will not be totally available to a FII having only income from the specified securities. Where the FII has in addition to income from specified Securities (including capital gains) income from other sources, it will no doubt be eligible to the deductions permitted under Chapter VI-A. However, some of the deductions (like donations under section 80G) are based on the gross total income, while there is a general ceiling to the effect that the aggregate of all deductions allowed under Chapter VI-A should not exceed the gross total income. For the purpose of determining the gross total income for the aforesaid purposes, income from the specified securities (including capital gains) will stand excluded. In other words, only the "other income" will be treated as gross total income for the purpose of allowing deductions under Chapter VI-A.

So far as the second question is concerned, from the perusal of section 55(2), it emerges that there are four categories of capital assets enumerated in clauses (a), (aa ), (ab) and (b) of sub-section (2) of section 55. Clause (b) is residuary provision governing 'any other capital asset'. The instant case is concerned with the capital asset falling within the scope of sub-clause (aa ) and category (B) thereof. The bonus shares allotted without payment of consideration is an additional financial asset that falls within part (B) of clause (aa) and, therefore, in the normal course, the cost of acquisition shall be taken to be 'nil' in view of stipulations in sub-clause (iiia). But, in relation to clause (aa) asset, that principle of computation stands excluded by the phrases 'subject to the provisions of sub-clauses (i ) and (ii) of clause (b)'. These said expression 'subject to' is significant and it points to the applicable provision for the purpose of ascertaining the cost of acquisition of an asset falling under clause (aa). In other words, the rules of computation of cost laid down in various sub-clauses of clause (aa ) have been expressly made subject to the provisions of sub-clauses (i ) and (ii) of clause (b). Thus, in the case of a capital asset answering the description given in sub-clauses (i) and (ii) of clause (b ), the rules of computation laid down by those sub-clauses of clause (b) would prevail over the rules in the preceding clause (aa). The expression 'subject to the provisions of sub-clauses (i) and (ii ) of clause (b)' was advisedly introduced to extend the benefit of deduction of deemed cost of acquisition in respect of a capital asset of the nature specified in clause (aa), if it was acquired before 1-4-1981. Otherwise, there is no purpose in ordaining that the operation of clause (aa) is subject to the provisions of sub-clauses (i) and (ii) of clause (b). The 'capital asset' referred to in clause (b) takes within its fold the financial assets in the form of shares or other secure- ties as specified in clause (aa). It is clear from clause (b) of section 55(2) that in the case of a capital asset falling within the ambit of that clause, acquired before 1-4-1981, the cost of acquisition can be taken as fair market value of that asset as on 1-4-1981. This provision prevails over sub-clause (iiia) of clause (aa). The applicant is, therefore, entitled to the benefit conferred by clause (b)(i ), of section 55(2). [Para 14]

Accordingly, the fair market value prevailing on 1-4-1981 ought to be taken as the cost of acquisition in the case of bonus shares held by the applicant on 1-4-1981. [Para 15]

The issue before the Hon'ble Bombay High Court was whether the alleged shortfall in share premium arising out of the issuance of shares by VISPL to VTSHL would constitute "income" chargeable to tax in the hands of VISPL.

2.2 Decisions in the case : 2.2-1 Whether TPO had jurisdiction where no income arose - The Hon'ble High Court relying on its earlier decision6 held as follows :

"A plain reading of Section 92(1) of the Act very clearly brings out that income arising from a International Transaction is a condition precedent for the application of Chapter X of the Act."

It rejected the revenue's contention that the question of examining the issue of jurisdiction did not arise because the impugned transaction was reported as an 'international transaction' in Form 3CEB, stating that the report was made exabundanticautela, just to inform the Revenue about the international transaction of issue of share capital while expressly denying that no income arose from such transaction.

Explaining the objective of Chapter X of the Act, the Hon'ble High Court observed that Transfer Pricing provisions ensure that in an international transaction between associated enterprises, neither the profits were understated nor the losses were overstated. They do not replace the concept of 'income' or 'expenditure', as normally understood in the Act, for the purposes of Chapter X. Their objective was not to punish multinational companies for doing business with their associated enterprises. Similarly, ALP was meant to determine the real value of the transaction and did not warrant recomputation of a capital receipt.

2.2-2 Whether income would include capital receipts? - On the issue, whether income as defined in Section 2(24) includes a capital receipt, the Hon'ble High Court held thus:

"We find considerable substance in the Petitioner's case that neither the capital receipts received by the Petitioner on issue of equity shares to its holding company, a non-resident entity, nor the alleged shortfall between the so called fair market price of its equity shares and the issue price of the equity shares can be considered as income within the meaning of the expression as defined under the Act."

It relied on its decision in Cadell Weaving Mill Co. v. CIT 7 as upheld by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in CIT v. D.P. Sandhu Bros. Chembur (P) Ltd.8 wherein it was held thus:

"…a capital receipt is not income under section 2(24), unless it is chargeable to tax as capital gains under section 45"

Further, the Hon'ble High Court rejected the contention of the Revenue to widen the meaning of the word 'income' to include all incomes. It referred to the test for interpreting a taxing statute laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Mathuram Agarwal v. State of M.P.9 holding that it was not open to the DRP to seek aid of the supposed intent of the Legislature to give a wider meaning to the word income. It emphasized on that a taxing statute had to be interpreted strictly. Words could not be added or substituted in order to give such a meaning as would serve to obtain the economic purpose or the spirit of the Legislature. The meaning had to be obtained from the plain language of a taxing statute. If there was ambiguity with regard to either the subject of the tax, the person liable to pay the tax or the rate of tax to be paid, then there was no tax chargeable under that law.

The High Court further held that "the transaction on capital account or on account of restructuring would become taxable to the extent it impacted income, i.e., under reporting of interest or over-reporting of interest paid or claiming of depreciation, etc. It is this income which is to be adjusted to the ALP price. It is not a tax on capital receipts." To this extent it was held that "the reliance by the revenue upon the definition of International Taxation in the sub-clauses (c) and (e) of Explanation (i) to Section 92B of the Act to conclude that Income has to be given a broader meaning to include notional income, as otherwise Chapter X of the Act would be rendered otiose is far fetched."

2.2-3 Whether notional income could be taxed? - On the Revenue's contention of charging to tax potential income, the High Court held that "In any case, the entire exercise of charging to tax the amounts allegedly not received as share premium fails, as no tax is being charged on the amount received as share premium."

It was argued on the Revenue's side that a conjoint reading of sub-clause (1) and sub-clause (2) of Section 92 of the Act indicates that what is sought to be taxed is the cost incurred in passing on the benefit to the holding company and not the share premium received. It was highlighted that the difference between the ALP and the price charged for the issue of shares was the benefit being passed on to VTSHL. The High Court held thus:

Broadly speaking, the issues involved in the controversy under study here can be summarized as:

A.

Whether issue of share capital/share infusion, not affecting the taxable income, can be regarded as an international transaction, under Chapter X?

B.

Whether the arm's length price of the issue of share capital, not affecting taxable income, is required to be computed under Chapter X? Whether Chapter X are machinery provisions?

C.

Impact of sections 56(2)(viia) and (viib) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 on the controversy.

2. IS SHARE INFUSION AN 'INTERNATIONAL TRANSACTION'?

Section 922 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (the Act) requires that any income, allowance for any expenses (including allocations) and allowance for any interest, arising out of international transactions should be computed having regard to the arm's length price.

The question is whether share infusion falls within the definition of the term 'international transaction' under section 92B of the Act. It may be mentioned that the term 'international transaction' as originally defined covered a wide gamut of transactions (including transactions having a bearing on assets) entered into between two associated enterprises (out of which, at least one should be a non-resident). By the Finance Act, 2010, an explanation was added to further extend the scope of this term. This extended definition was made retrospectively effective from the day the Indian Transfer Pricing Regulations were introduced i.e. April 1, 2001.

This extended definition includes a clause, which reads as follows:

'(e) a transaction of business restructuring or reorganisation, entered into by an enterprise with an associated enterprise, irrespective of the fact that it has bearing on the profit, income, losses or assets of such enterprises at the time of the transaction or at any future date'

The term 'business restructuring' or 'reorganisation' have not been defined in the Act and hence prone to a wider interpretation. It is possible that the tax department may seek to infer that these terms cover any change in shareholding, including share infusion. Even without resorting to the extension of the definition, a view is possible that 'share' is a form of an 'assets' and hence, any change in the value of shares, would impact the assets of a taxpayer. Therefore, it can be said that share infusion stands covered by the original definition of the term international transaction.

3. WHETHER ARM'S LENGTH PRICE OF ISSUE OF SHARE CAPITAL IS REQUIRED TO BE COMPUTED UNDER CHAPTER X? WHETHER CHAPTER X ARE MACHINERY PROVISIONS?

To answer this question, one needs to refer to section 92 of the Act. It requires that income, expense and interest in relation to an international transaction should be computed having regard to the arm's length price. Thus, the primary question is: whether infusion of share capital can be regarded as income?

This was addressed by VISPL's counsel before the Bombay High Court. In brief, the prime contention of VISPL's counsel was:

The term 'income' is defined under section 2(24) of the Act. A perusal of the Act shows that nowhere, any shortfall on account of share infusion, is treated as income. If a case does not fall under section 56(2)(viib) of the Act (discussed later), even share premium in excess of fair market value of shares cannot be treated as income.

3. Preference shareholder cannot maintain an insolvency petition u/s 7 as CRPS funds are share capital not debt: SC

EPC Constructions India Ltd. v. Matix Fertilizers and Chemicals Ltd. [2025] 179 taxmann.com 650 (SC) In the instant case, the appellant, acting as an engineering, procurement and construction contractor, had entered into contracts with the respondent for setting up a fertiliser complex, under which an amount of about ?572.7 crores became due. The parties thereafter discussed conversion of a part of the outstanding receivables into a subordinate debt. Pursuant to this, the respondent proposed conversion of up to ?400 crores of the outstanding dues into preference shares.

The appellant's board approved conversion into 8% Cumulative Redeemable Preference Shares (CRPS), and the respondent allotted 25 crore CRPS of ?10 each aggregating to ?250 crores, carrying a cumulative dividend of 8% and redeemable at par at the end of three years, with an option to redeem earlier at the issuer's discretion. The appellant accepted the allotment and the CRPS were issued accordingly.

On expiry of the redemption period, the appellant filed an application under section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code claiming about ?310 crores as payable on maturity of the CRPS. The NCLT dismissed the application, and the NCLAT, by the impugned order, dismissed the appeal.

The Supreme Court held that the fact that the redemption period of the CRPS had expired did not lend greater weight to the appellant's case. It held that the appellant, being a preference shareholder, was not a creditor and, therefore, an application under section 7 was not maintainable. The Court further held that accounting treatment of the transaction, based on accounting standards, would not be determinative of the nature of the relationship between the parties, which had to be gathered from the documents executed between them.

The Court held that the paid-up money on shares constitutes share capital and does not amount to debt. It further held that shares could be redeemed only out of profits or out of amounts set aside for payment of dividends, which was not the situation in the present case, and therefore the argument that redemption was due was not meritorious. Accordingly, the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal.

4. Rights issue during CD's CIRP valid; plea to restrain EGM and alteration of CD's shareholding dismissed: SC

Glas Trust Company LLC v. Shailendra Ajmera [2025] 180 taxmann.com 524 (SC)

In the instant case, the corporate debtor held about 25.41 per cent shareholding in company 'A' and was admitted into the corporate insolvency resolution process. The resolution professional did not attend meetings of the board of company 'A'. Thereafter, company 'A' passed a resolution to increase its share capital through a rights issue at face value and issued a notice convening an extraordinary general meeting of its shareholders.

An appellant, being a shareholder of the corporate debtor, filed an application seeking an interim injunction to restrain company 'A' from convening its extraordinary general meeting and from reducing the shareholding of the corporate debtor. It was noted that the proposed increase in share capital was through a rights issue and not by way of a public offer. Consequently, the corporate debtor, as a shareholder, would be entitled to subscribe to shares in proportion to its existing shareholding of 25.41 per cent.

The NCLAT held that if the corporate debtor considered it necessary to sustain the value of its investment or to retain any control arising from its shareholding in company 'A', it was open to it to subscribe to the shares offered under the rights issue. If the committee of creditors chose not to subscribe to the shares, the resultant change in shareholding would be a consequence of its own decision and not attributable to company 'A'. The Tribunal further held that, notwithstanding the order of status quo passed by the NCLT, the decision impacting the shareholding of the corporate debtor rested with it and not with company 'A'. Accordingly, the application seeking to restrain the extraordinary general meeting and the dilution of shareholding was dismissed.

The Supreme Court declined to interfere with the impugned order passed by the NCLAT. It held that the observations made by the Tribunal were only for the purpose of disposal of the interim application and would not have any bearing on the final adjudication of the appeal pending before the Tribunal.

2.2-4 Applicability of Chapter X to Share Subscription - With respect to applicability of Transfer Pricing provisions to share subscription the High Court observed as under :

Thus, such a capital account transaction not falling within a statutory exception cannot be brought to tax"

Referring to the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Bombay Tyres India Ltd. v. Union of India10, it was held that arriving at the value of transaction on the basis of ALP would not convert non-income to income. Tax could be charged only on income and where income would not arise, the point of applying ALP to measure the value of the transaction itself would not arise.

The Hon'ble High Court further observed that the Parliament had consciously not brought to tax amounts received from a non-resident for issue of shares under Section 56(2)(viib) of the Act, as it would discourage capital inflow from abroad. The High Court went on to hold that, although Section 56(1) of the Act would allow, under the head 'income from other sources', all income which is not otherwise excluded, it does not provide for charging to tax capital receipts in respect of issue of shares as it has been specifically provided for in Section 45 or Section 56(2)(viib) of the Act.

It further explained that while income is a flow, capital is a fund. The decision of the Privy Council in CIT v. Shaw Wallace & Co. Ltd.11 was referred to by the High Court to bring out this distinction, wherein it was observed thus:

"…income has been likened pictorially to the fruit of a tree or the crop of a field. It is essentially the produce of something which is often loosely spoken of as capital"

The High Court further rejected the contention that Chapter X was a complete Code by itself. It held thus:

"It is well-settled position, in law, that a charge to tax must be found specifically mentioned in the Act. In the absence of there being a charging Section in Chapter X of the Act, it is not possible to read a charging provision into Chapter X of the Act."

Relying on the Constitutional Bench's Judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in CIT v. Vatika Township (P.) Ltd.12, the High Court held that there was no charge whether express or implied, in letter or in spirit, to tax the issue of shares at a premium. The High Court also referred to the decision of the Supreme Court in CIT v. B.C. Srinivasa Shetty13 to explain that the difference between charging provisions and computing provisions is qualitative in nature and computation provisions cannot substitute the charging provisions. In B.C. Srinivasa Shetty14, the transaction was not taxed as, even though there was a charging provision, yet the computation provision failed. The High Court concluded that the facts of the instant case were on a higher pedestal as there was no charging provision to tax issue of shares at premium to a non-resident, thus, there could be no occasion to invoke computational provisions.

Conclusion 3. As is evidenced from the above analysis, the Bombay High Court has certainly brought to rest many questions vexing Multi-national Corporations in regard to subscription of shares to their associated enterprises. It has reaffirmed that income does not arise from capital receipts and that there could be no taxation on notional income. It has further clarified that if income does not arise out of an international transaction, then the TPO has no jurisdiction to compute the ALP. Chapter X of the Act consists of machinery provisions. Charging provisions cannot be read into it in the absence of a specific charging section under the Act. Issuance of shares to fund subsidiaries is common-place in Multi-national Corporations and is globally considered to be away from the clutches of Transfer Pricing. In the Indian context, the instant ruling has ended the controversy. The tides of Transfer Pricing should no longer cause worry in the minds of foreign investors from infusing more funds in their Indian subsidiaries. It is a welcome decision that clearly draws the line where the applicability of Chapter X of the Act is restricted. However, it remains to be seen whether the Revenue will further agitate this issue in the Apex Court or lays it to rest after this reasoned decision of the Hon'ble Bombay High Court.

19. Excess share premium not taxable in hands of closely held co. if its shareholders are relatives: ITAT

[Vaani Estates (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [2018] 98 taxmann.com 92 (Chennai - Trib.)] The assessee-company had only two shareholders 'S' and her husband. On passing away of husband, his shares devolved on their daughter 'V'. The assessee proposed to acquire an immovable property at approximately Rs. 23.09 crores. 'S' brought in money into the company in lieu of allotment of fresh 10,100 shares with a share premium of Rs. 23.31 crores.

The Assessing Officer opined that company had received excess price/share premium for the shares allotted to 'S' over and above the face value of shares. Accordingly, he brought Rs. 23.31 crores to tax in the hands of the company under Section 56(2)(viib).

The ITAT held in favour of assessee as under:

When 'S' introduced money into the company for allotment of shares at an exorbitant premium in contrast to its intrinsic value of just Rs. 10 per share, the benefit of such investment had only passed on to her daughter because there were only two shareholders in the company at that point of time. Had 'S' gifted the money to her daughter 'V' and thereafter if daughter had brought the same into the company for allotment of equity shares at face value, question of invoking of the provisions of section 56(2)(viib) would not have arisen.

Provisions of section 56(2)(viib) couldn't be invoked in the case of the assessee-co. because by virtue of introducing cash in the company by 'S' for allotment of equity shares with unrealistic premium the benefit had only passed on to her daughter 'V' and there was no scope in the Act to tax when cash or asset was transferred by a mother to her daughter.

20. No concealment penalty if assessee has bona fide belief that notional income isn't taxable: ITAT

[DCIT v. Shah Rukh Khan [2018] 93 taxmann.com 320 (Mumbai - Trib.)]

The assessee, Mr. Shah Rukh Khan, had received a villa at Dubai as gift and offered an amount of Rs. 14 lakhs as the notional income of the villa for tax in his return of income for the year under consideration. During the course of assessment proceedings, assessee claimed that Article 6 of India-UAE tax treaty doesn't expressly recognize the right of the resident State to tax the income from immovable property situated in the source State. Therefore, the notional income of the villa owned by him in Dubai could not be subjected to tax in India.

The ITAT held that claim raised by the assessee being clearly backed up by a bonafide belief on his part that the notional income of the villa was not liable to be taxed in India, no penalty for concealment of income could be validly imposed on the assessee.

21. Australia has taxing rights under Australia-India DTAA even if there is no provision in its domestic law: Australian Court

[Satyam Computer Services Ltd. (Now Tech Mahindra Limited) v. Commissioner of Taxation [2018] 98 taxmann.com 358 (FC-Australia)]

The Applicant, Tech Mahindra, had offices in Sydney and Melbourne through which it provided software products and information technology services to entities in Australia. Payments received by applicant for the services provided in Australia by the employees located in India were treated as 'Royalties' as per Article 12(3)(g) of the Australia-India DTAA .

Applicant argued that, though Australia was allocated the right to tax the 'Royalties' by the Indian Agreement but it could only exercise that right if it had the right to impose tax on those amounts under Australia's domestic law. As of now, the domestic law does not give any right to Australia to tax such income.

The Federal Court of Australia held as under:

The language of Article 23 should be given effect to according to its terms and the context. Article 23 provides that that income derived by a resident of one contracting States may be deemed to be income from sources in other contracting state for purpose of law of that other State. Therefore, royalty income was to be included in the applicant's assessable income because it was income from an Australian source by reason of Article 23 of the Australia-India DTAA. The Court rejected the argument that the tax treaties can only be used as shields not swords. It held that the tax treaties also provide standalone taxing power and independent imposing of tax to a particular income.

Whether capital account transaction could be charged to tax: The amount received on issue of shares is admittedly a capital account transaction not separately brought within the definition of Income, except in cases covered by Section 56(2)(viib) of the Act. Thus, such capital account transaction not falling within a statutory exception could not be brought to tax.In tax jurisprudence, it is well-settled that following four factors are essential ingredients to a taxing statute:

(a)

Subject of tax;

(b)

Person liable to pay the tax;

(c)

Rate at which tax is to be paid, and

(d)

Measure or value on which the rate is to be applied.

There is difference between a charge to tax and the measure of tax as mentioned in (a) and (d) above. This distinction was brought out by the Supreme Court in Bombay Tyres India Ltd. v. Union of India [1984] 1 SCC 467 wherein it was held that the charge of excise duty is on manufacture while the measure of the tax is the selling price of the manufactured goods.

In this case, the charge was on income as understood in the Act, and where income arises from an International Transaction, than the measure is to be found on application of ALP so far Chapter X of the Act is concerned.

Thus, arriving at the transactional value/consideration on the basis of ALP does not convert non-income into income. The tax can be charged only on income and in the absence of any income arising, the issue of applying the measure of ALP to transactional value/consideration itself does not arise.

The ingredient (a) above is not satisfied, i.e., subject of tax is income which is chargeable to tax. The issue of shares at a premium is a capital account transaction and not income.

(b)

Whether Chapter X of the Income-tax Act includes a charging provision to tax issue of shares at a premium as income: On contention of the revenue that Chapter X of the Act is a complete Code by itself and not merely a machinery provision to compute the ALP and, therefore, hidden benefit arising out of the transaction of issue shares to AE should be charged to tax as the charging section is inherent in Chapter X of the Act, the High Court held as under:

i.

It is well-settled position, in law, that a charge to tax must be mentioned specifically in the Act. In the absence of there being a charging Section in Chapter X of the Act, it is not possible to read a charging provision into Chapter X of the Act. There is no charge express or implied in letter or in spirit to tax issue of shares at a premium as income.

ii.

Chapter X of the Act is a machinery provision to arrive at the ALP of a transaction between AEs. The substantive charging provisions are found in Sections 4, 5, 15 (Salaries), 22 (Income from house property), 28 (Profits and gains of business), 45 (Capital gain) and 56 (Income from other Sources).

iii.

Even Income arising from International Transaction between AE must satisfy the test of Income under the Act and must find its home in one of the above heads, i.e., charging provisions which revenue had not been able to show.

iv.

In the present case, there was no charging provision to tax capital account transaction in respect of issue of shares at a premium and computation provisions could not replace/ substitute the charging provisions.

v.

Thus, issue of shares at a premium by Vodafone to its non-resident holding company did not give rise to any income from an admitted International Transaction. So, no occasion to apply Chapter X of the Act can arise in such a case.

17. Reopening of cases of Rahul Gandhi and Sonia Gandhi is valid as they failed to disclose shares allotted in excess of FMV: HC

[Sonia Gandhi v. ACIT [2018] 97 taxmann.com 150 (Delhi)]

The assessees, Mr. Rahul Gandhi and Mrs. Sonia Gandhi, extended a loan to the National Herald to write off the accumulated debts and recommence the newspaper publication. The said loan was assigned by the assessee to a newly incorporated non-profit company 'Young India' (YI) and in lieu of that they were allotted shares of YI. However, in Income-tax returns, they failed to pay tax on the shares allotted by Young India. The assessees argued that the allotment of shares did not trigger any taxing event. It was also argued that since they were shareholders of a non-profit and charitable company, they were under no obligation to disclose the value of shares.

The High Court held in favour of revenue that sub-clause (ii) of clause (c) of Section 56(2) provides that if certain shares or property are acquired at a price which is less than its aggregate fair market value by an amount exceeding Rs. 50,000, the fair market value as reduced by the considered paid shall be charged to tax. In the instant case, the assessee bought the shares at Rs. 100 per share which could not be deemed as its fair market value. The assesse had nowhere disclosed the fair market value of such shares and had not recorded the facts relating to above taxing event. Further, it couldn't be held that the individual was exempted altogether from disclosing her or his interest in the acquisition of shares merely because shares were of not-for-profit Company. Therefore, the AO was justified in reopening the cases.
